knowledge_statements.statement_title: P-BDR yields an exact semidefinite convex-hull representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact moment and localizing-matrix lift of a compact basic semialgebraic set's convex hull under P-BDR.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\geq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be compact and suppose P-BDR holds for \(K\) with order \(d\). Then \(\operatorname{co}(K)\) is semidefinite representable and \[\operatorname{co}(K)=\left\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^{s(2d)},\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ M_{d-v_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ L_y(1)=1,\ L_y(x_i)=z_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n)\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a compact basic semialgebraic set has P-BDR of order d, its convex hull is exactly the projection of the corresponding order-d moment and localizing-matrix system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{co}(K)=\left\{z:\exists y,\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ M_{d-v_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\ \forall j,\ L_y(1)=1,\ L_y(x_i)=z_i\ \forall i\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stengle’s Certificate for Emptiness of a Semialgebraic Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed polynomial inequalities, inequations, and equations over a real closed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a real closed field and let \(F=(f_i)_{i\in I_1}\), \(G=(g_i)_{i\in I_2}\), and \(H=(h_i)_{i\in I_3}\) be finite families in \(k[\mathbf{x}]\). Let \(P(F)\) be the preordering generated by \(F\), \(M(G)\) the multiplicative monoid of finite products of elements of \(G\), including \(1\), and \(I(H)\) the ideal generated by \(H\). Then \[K:=\{\mathbf{x}\in k^n:f_i(\mathbf{x})\ge0\ \forall i\in I_1,\ g_i(\mathbf{x})\ne0\ \forall i\in I_2,\ h_i(\mathbf{x})=0\ \forall i\in I_3\}\] is empty if and only if there exist \(f\in P(F)\), \(g\in M(G)\), and \(h\in I(H)\) such that \(f+g^2+h=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite mixed semialgebraic system over a real closed field is infeasible exactly when its preordering, inequation monoid, and equality ideal supply an identity of the form f plus g squared plus h equals zero.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is a real closed field}
F\cup G\cup H\subset k[\mathbf{x}]\text{ consists of finite indexed families}
K=\{\mathbf{x}\in k^n:f_i(\mathbf{x})\ge0,\ g_i(\mathbf{x})\ne0,\ h_i(\mathbf{x})=0\text{ for all corresponding indices}\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=\varnothing\iff\exists f\in P(F),\ g\in M(G),\ h\in I(H):\ f+g^2+h=0

knowledge_statements.title: Saturated Quadratic Modules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines saturation relative to the positivity set associated with a quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\) be a quadratic module and let \(K_M=\{a\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(a)\ge0\text{ for every }f\in M\}\). Its saturation is \(\operatorname{Sat}(M)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[x]:f(a)\ge0\text{ for every }a\in K_M\}\). The module \(M\) is saturated precisely when \[M=\operatorname{Sat}(M).\] Equivalently, every polynomial nonnegative on \(K_M\), including polynomials vanishing on its boundary, already has a certificate belonging to \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic module is saturated when it contains every polynomial nonnegative on its associated positivity set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is saturated if and only if \(M=\operatorname{Sat}(M)\).

notation.meaning: Positivity set associated with the module.
Cone of all polynomials nonnegative on the positivity set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set dependence, closedness, and compactness consequences intrinsic to a saturated quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a saturated quadratic module. Since \(M=\operatorname{Pos}(K_M)\), it is determined solely by \(K_M\) and is closed in the finest locally convex topology. Moreover, \(M\) is Archimedean if and only if \(K_M\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saturated quadratic module is the closed nonnegativity cone of its set and is Archimedean exactly when that set is compact.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=\operatorname{Pos}(K_M),\quad M\text{ is closed},\quad[M\text{ Archimedean}\iff K_M\text{ compact}]

knowledge_statements.title: Saturated Preorderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines saturation of a preordering by its associated nonnegativity cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\) be a preordering and define \(K_T=\{a\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(a)\ge0\text{ for every }f\in T\}\). Its saturation is \(\operatorname{Sat}(T)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[x]:f(a)\ge0\text{ for every }a\in K_T\}\). The preordering \(T\) is saturated when \[T=\operatorname{Sat}(T).\] For a finitely generated preordering \(T(g)\), this means that every polynomial nonnegative on \(K(g)\) admits a representation by sums of squares multiplied by squarefree products of the generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preordering is saturated when its certificates represent every polynomial nonnegative on the associated basic closed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is saturated if and only if \(T=\operatorname{Sat}(T)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Archimedean Square Module That Is Not Saturated
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit regime representing every strictly positive polynomial while missing a boundary-vanishing nonnegative polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\Sigma[x,y]+(1-x^2)\Sigma[x,y]+(1-y^2)\Sigma[x,y]\). Then \(K_M=[-1,1]^2\) and \(2-x^2-y^2\in M\), so \(M\) is Archimedean and every polynomial strictly positive on \([-1,1]^2\) belongs to \(M\). Nevertheless, \(h=(1-x^2)(1-y^2)\) is nonnegative on \([-1,1]^2\) but does not belong to \(M\). Thus \(M\) is not saturated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Archimedean quadratic module generated by the two square constraints represents every strictly positive polynomial on the square but omits their nonnegative product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{f:f>0\text{ on }[-1,1]^2\}\subseteq M,\qquad(1-x^2)(1-y^2)\in\operatorname{Pos}([-1,1]^2)\setminus M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Positivity Membership Does Not Imply Saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact logical boundary between representing strictly positive and all nonnegative polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a quadratic module or preordering with positivity set \(K_C\). Suppose every polynomial strictly positive on \(K_C\) belongs to \(C\), but \(C\neq\operatorname{Pos}(K_C)\). Then there exists \(h\geq0\) on \(K_C\) with \(h\notin C\), and every such witness has a zero on \(K_C\); otherwise it would be strictly positive and hence belong to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict-positivity theorem can hold without saturation, and every missing nonnegative polynomial must vanish somewhere on the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists h\in\operatorname{Pos}(K_C)\setminus C,\qquad\min_{x\in K_C}h(x)=0

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Membership Does Not Imply Saturation
Strict Positivity Without Saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes strict-positivity representation from representation of boundary-vanishing polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\) be a quadratic module or preordering with positivity set \(K_C\). A strict-positivity theorem may establish \(\{f:f>0\text{ on }K_C\}\subseteq C\) while \(C\) remains nonsaturated. Nonsaturation is witnessed by some \(h\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) satisfying \(h\ge0\) on \(K_C\) but \(h\notin C\); such a witness must attain zero on \(K_C\), because a strictly positive witness would lie in \(C\). Thus strict positivity does not settle exact representation on the boundary of the nonnegativity cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representing every strictly positive polynomial need not represent all nonnegative polynomials; any missing polynomial must vanish somewhere on the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) represents every polynomial strictly positive on \(K_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(h\ge0\) on \(K_C\) with \(h\notin C\), and every such \(h\) has a zero on \(K_C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the nonnegative-coefficient certificate cone generated by normalized constraints and their complements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{\mathbf x:g_j(\mathbf x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be compact. For each \(j\), let \(\bar g_j:=\sup_{\mathbf x\in K}g_j(\mathbf x)\) and define \(\widehat g_j:=g_j/\bar g_j\) when \(\bar g_j>0\), and \(\widehat g_j:=g_j\) when \(\bar g_j=0\). Let \(G=(0,1,\widehat g_1,\ldots,\widehat g_m,1-\widehat g_1,\ldots,1-\widehat g_m)\). The cone \(C_G\) generated by finite products of elements of \(G\) is the set of all finite sums \(\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^m}c_{\alpha\beta}\widehat{\mathbf g}^{\alpha}(\mathbf1-\widehat{\mathbf g})^{\beta}\) with \(c_{\alpha\beta}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each constraint is normalized by its supremum on the compact feasible set when that supremum is positive. The cone consists of finite nonnegative-coefficient polynomials in the normalized constraints and their complements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_G=\left\{\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^m}c_{\alpha\beta}\widehat{\mathbf g}^{\alpha}(\mathbf1-\widehat{\mathbf g})^{\beta}:c_{\alpha\beta}\ge0\text{ and finitely supported}\right\}

children.title: Stable Certificate Cones
children.top_down_role: Certificate systems admitting structured degree control.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Presentation-sensitive bounded-degree definition for a fixed weighted-SOS cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a weighted-SOS presentation of a cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\). Let \(C_{\le N}\) contain the elements admitting a certificate in which every weighted term has degree at most \(N\). The presentation is stable if, for every \(d\), there exists \(N(d)\) such that \[C\cap\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}=C_{\le N(d)}\cap\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}.\] Thus every cone member of input degree at most \(d\) has a certificate-degree bound depending only on \(d\) and the fixed presentation, not on its coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed certificate presentation is stable when every bounded input-degree slice of the full cone is captured by one uniformly bounded certificate truncation.
assumptions_latex: The generators and weighted-term degree convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall d\,\exists N(d):C\cap\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}=C_{\le N(d)}\cap\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}.

notation.meaning: uniform certificate-degree bound for input degree d

knowledge_statements.title: Filtration Definition of Certificate-Cone Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical stable certificate presentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a<b\), the univariate preordering generated by \(x-a\) and \(b-x\), with weighted-term degree as the filtration, is stable. The Markov–Lukács representations show that every polynomial \(f\ge0\) on \([a,b]\) has a certificate whose weighted terms have degree at most \(\deg f\). Hence one may take \(N(d)=d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard univariate interval preordering is stable with certificate degree bounded linearly by input degree.
assumptions_latex: The standard interval generators and weighted-term degree convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(d)=d\text{ is a valid stability bound for the interval preordering.}
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Preordering Is Stable
Stable Certificate Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-filtration definition for finitely generated polynomial certificate cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\) be a finitely generated quadratic module or preordering, with its fixed generators and standard certificate form. The cone \(C\) is stable if, for every integer \(d\ge0\), there exists an integer \(N(d)\) such that every \(f\in C\) with \(\deg f\le d\) has a certificate in which every weighted sum-of-squares term has degree at most \(N(d)\). The bound may depend on \(C\) and \(d\), but not on the coefficients of the particular polynomial \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate cone is stable when bounded-degree members always possess certificates with a degree bound depending only on the input degree and fixed cone.
assumptions_latex: A fixed weighted sum-of-squares presentation of \(C\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stability is the existence of a uniform certificate-degree function \(N(d)\) for each input degree \(d\).

notation.meaning: Uniform certificate-degree bound for cone members of degree at most d.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed filtration-based definition is plausible, but stability conventions vary regarding generators and whether degree is measured termwise or through multiplier degrees. An authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Effective Positivstellensatz Regimes
children.top_down_role: Assumption classes supporting quantitative certificate-degree bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact univariate regime with certificate degree controlled by polynomial degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\) be nonnegative on \([a,b]\), where \(a<b\). If \(\deg f\le2m\), then \(f=s_0+(x-a)(b-x)s_1\), where \(s_0,s_1\) are sums of squares, \(\deg s_0\le2m\), and \(\deg s_1\le2m-2\). If \(\deg f\le2m+1\), then \(f=(x-a)s_0+(b-x)s_1\), where \(s_0,s_1\) are sums of squares with \(\deg s_i\le2m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every univariate polynomial nonnegative on a compact interval has an exact weighted-SOS certificate with degree controlled by its own degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ has the stated parity-dependent degree-controlled weighted-SOS representation.}
knowledge_statements.title: Markov–Lukács Effective Interval Certificate
Effective Positivstellensatz Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies what constitutes a quantitative, effective positivity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider rational input polynomials \(g_1,\ldots,g_m,f\in\mathbb{Q}[x]\), a certified compactness radius \(R\), and a certified margin \(\delta>0\) such that \(f(x)\ge\delta\) on \(K(g)\). An effective Positivstellensatz regime supplies an explicit computable function \(B\) of \(n\), \(m\), the input degrees and coefficient heights, \(R\), and \(\delta^{-1}\), such that \(f\) has the asserted quadratic-module or preordering certificate with every weighted term of degree at most \(B\). Truncation at order \(\lceil B/2\rceil\) then suffices to search for that certificate by semidefinite programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An effective regime gives a computable certificate-degree bound from dimensions, input size, compactness data, and a positive lower margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A certificate exists with weighted-term degree at most the explicit bound \(B\).

notation.meaning: Certified positivity margin on the feasible set.
Certified compactness radius or comparable size datum.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes what an effective bound would be but gives no actual function or theorem, so it does not yet justify the selected complexity_bound kind. A specific effective Positivstellensatz with its hypotheses, degree formula, encoding model, and locator is required.

children.title: Absence of Uniform Degree Bounds
children.top_down_role: Families where certificate existence does not provide uniform finite-degree control.

knowledge_statements.title: Absence of Uniform Degree Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence characterization of failure of certificate-cone stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\) be a fixed finitely generated quadratic module or preordering. Uniform degree control fails exactly when there exists an integer \(d\ge0\) and a sequence \((f_k)_{k\ge1}\subseteq C\) with \(\deg f_k\le d\) such that the minimum possible maximum degree of the weighted terms in any certificate of \(f_k\) tends to infinity as \(k\to\infty\). Hence membership of every \(f_k\) in \(C\) guarantees finite certificates individually but supplies no common finite truncation order for the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform degree bounds fail when fixed-degree cone members require certificates of arbitrarily increasing degree, despite each member having some finite certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\) is a fixed finitely generated certificate cone.
Certificate degree is measured by the largest weighted-term degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are \(d\) and \((f_k)\subseteq C\) with \(\deg f_k\le d\) but minimum certificate degree tending to infinity.

notation.meaning: Family of bounded-degree members of the certificate cone.
Common upper bound on polynomial degree.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequence formulation is a plausible negation of stability and the failure_boundary kind fits, but it inherits an unsourced degree convention and has no authoritative locator confirming the characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Certificate Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness in a specified locally convex topology on the polynomial coefficient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) carry a locally convex topology \(\tau\), and let \(C\subseteq A\) be a convex cone of algebraic certificates. The cone \(C\) is \(\tau\)-closed if every \(\tau\)-convergent net \((c_\alpha)\subseteq C\) has its limit in \(C\). Equivalently, \(C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\). Therefore every element of \(\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\) is an actual certificate whenever \(C\) is \(\tau\)-closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate cone is closed in the chosen topology when every convergent net of certificates has its limit in the cone, equivalently when taking its closure adds no elements.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq A\text{ is a convex cone}
\tau\text{ is a locally convex topology on }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-dual characterization of closed certificate cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex cone in a Hausdorff locally convex space \((V,\tau)\), and define \(C^*=\{\ell\in V'_\tau:\ell(c)\ge0\ \forall c\in C\}\). Then \(C^{**}=\operatorname{cl}_\tau C\). Consequently, \(C\) is \(\tau\)-closed if and only if \(C=C^{**}\), equivalently if every \(v\notin C\) admits a continuous linear functional \(\ell\) satisfying \(\ell(c)\ge0\) for all \(c\in C\) and \(\ell(v)<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex certificate cone is closed exactly when it equals its continuous bidual, equivalently when every exterior point has a continuous separating witness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is closed}\iff C=C^{**}\iff\text{every }v\notin C\text{ is continuously separated from }C.

children.title: Moment Property
children.top_down_role: Certificate-cone regimes whose positive functionals admit representing measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary moment property; representing measures need not be supported on the positivity set of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a convex cone containing all squares, and define \(M^\vee=\{L\in A^*:L(m)\geq0\ \text{for every }m\in M\}\). The cone \(M\) has the moment property if every \(L\in M^\vee\) is a moment functional: there exists a positive Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with all polynomial moments finite, such that \(L(f)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\,d\mu(x)\) for every \(f\in A\). No support restriction beyond \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The moment property says every linear functional nonnegative on the certificate cone is integration against a positive measure on the ambient real space.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq A\text{ is a convex cone containing all squares}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^\vee\subseteq\{L_\mu:\mu\text{ is a positive Borel measure on }\mathbb{R}^n\}

notation.meaning: polynomial integration functional induced by a measure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Characterization of the Moment Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipolar characterization for a sound certificate cone in the finest locally convex topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) carry its finest locally convex topology, let \(P=\operatorname{Pos}(\mathbb R^n)\), and let \(M\subseteq P\) be a convex cone. Then \(M\) has the moment property if and only if \(\operatorname{cl}M=P\). Equivalently, \(M^\vee=P^\vee\), and Riesz–Haviland identifies \(P^\vee\) with the polynomial integration functionals induced by positive Borel measures having all moments finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound certificate cone has the moment property exactly when it is dense in the global nonnegativity cone in the finest locally convex topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Moment Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-sensitive moment property for a polynomial certificate cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(M\subseteq A=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), set \(K_M=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:m(x)\geq0\ \text{for every }m\in M\}\). The cone \(M\) has the strong moment property if every linear functional \(L:A\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(L(m)\geq0\) for all \(m\in M\) admits a positive Borel representing measure \(\mu\) with all moments finite and \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq K_M\), such that \(L(f)=\int_{K_M}f(x)\,d\mu(x)\) for every \(f\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong moment property requires every cone-positive functional to have a representing measure supported on the cone's associated positivity set.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq A\text{ is a convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^\vee\subseteq\{L_\mu:\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq K_M\}

children.title: Nonclosed Certificate Cones
children.top_down_role: Certificate settings where limiting cone elements need not remain certified.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Certificate Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological failure separating limiting certificates from exact certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex certificate cone in a locally convex space \((V,\tau)\). The cone is nonclosed precisely when \(C\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\). Equivalently, there exist \(v\in V\setminus C\) and a net \((c_\alpha)\subseteq C\) that converges to \(v\) in \(\tau\). Thus \(v\) is a limiting certificate but has no exact certificate belonging to \(C\), which is the basic closure-related boundary for certificate attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate cone is nonclosed when a net of certificates converges to an element outside the cone, so a limiting certificate need not be an exact certificate in the cone.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq V\text{ is a convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C

notation.meaning: topological closure of the certificate cone
limiting object without an exact certificate in C

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Relative Interior and Closure p. 7

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Relative Interior and Closure p. 7

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete sequence demonstrating nonclosure without importing positivity or moment-representation failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{(x,0):x\ge0\}\) is a convex cone but is not closed. Indeed, \((-1,1/n)\in C\) for every \(n\), whereas \((-1,1/n)\to(-1,0)\notin C\). Interpreting membership in \(C\) as an abstract certificate condition, exact certificates exist along the sequence but not at its limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple convex cone contains every point (−1,1/n) but not their limit (−1,0).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}C.
knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Nonclosed Convex Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous-polar relationship between a convex cone and its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any convex cone \(C\) in a locally convex space, \(C^*=(\operatorname{cl}C)^*\) and \(C^{**}=\operatorname{cl}C\), where polars are taken in the continuous dual pairing. Hence every continuous functional nonnegative on \(C\) is also nonnegative on its closure; continuous dual inequalities cannot distinguish an exact certificate in \(C\) from a merely limiting certificate in \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone and its closure have the same continuous dual cone, so continuous dual inequalities cannot distinguish exact from limiting certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a locally convex space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^*=(\operatorname{cl}C)^*\quad\text{and}\quad C^{**}=\operatorname{cl}C.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Functionals Cannot Detect Nonclosure

children.title: Positivity Outside Cone Closure
children.top_down_role: Positive polynomials lying beyond the closure of the selected certificate cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Motzkin Polynomial Outside the SOS Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical instantiated failure for the global SOS cone in the finest locally convex topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\Sigma[x,y]\) and \(m(x,y)=x^4y^2+x^2y^4-3x^2y^2+1\). Then \(K_M=\mathbb R^2\), the Motzkin polynomial \(m\) is globally nonnegative, and \(m\notin M\). In the finest locally convex topology on \(\mathbb R[x,y]\), the SOS cone is closed because its intersection with each finite-degree coefficient space is closed; hence \(m\in\operatorname{Pos}(\mathbb R^2)\setminus\operatorname{cl}M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The globally nonnegative Motzkin polynomial lies outside the closed global SOS cone.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb R[x,y]\text{ carries its finest locally convex topology}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m\in\operatorname{Pos}(\mathbb R^2)\setminus\operatorname{cl}M

notation.meaning: cone of sums of squares in R[x,y]

knowledge_statements.title: Motzkin Polynomial Outside the SOS Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positivity Outside a Specified Cone Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-explicit definition of failure of a closed certificate cone to capture feasible-set nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) carry a topology \(\tau\), let \(M\subseteq A\) be a certificate cone, and set \(K_M=\{x:m(x)\geq0\ \forall m\in M\}\). Positivity outside the \(\tau\)-closure of \(M\) occurs when \(\operatorname{Pos}(K_M)\nsubseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}M\), equivalently when some \(f\geq0\) on \(K_M\) satisfies \(f\notin\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure occurs when a polynomial nonnegative on the associated set cannot even be approximated by certificates in the specified topology.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\text{ is a certificate cone}
\tau\text{ is a specified topology on the polynomial space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Pos}(K_M)\nsubseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}M

notation.meaning: closure of M in the specified topology

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity Outside a Specified Cone Closure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual characterization after fixing a Hausdorff locally convex topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space, let \(M\subseteq A\) be a convex cone, and let \(f\in A\). Then \(f\notin\operatorname{cl}M\) if and only if there exists a continuous linear functional \(L\in A'\) such that \(L(m)\geq0\) for every \(m\in M\) and \(L(f)<0\). Thus every \(f\in\operatorname{Pos}(K_M)\setminus\operatorname{cl}M\) has a continuous M-positive separating witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial outside the closed certificate cone is detected by a continuous cone-positive functional that evaluates it negatively.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is a Hausdorff locally convex real topological vector space}
M\subseteq A\text{ is a convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\notin\operatorname{cl}M\iff\exists L\in A':L(M)\geq0\text{ and }L(f)<0

notation.meaning: continuous dual for the specified topology

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Separation from Cone Closure
Positivity Outside Cone Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a certificate cone, even after closure, to capture all nonnegative polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq A=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a certificate cone, let \(K_M=\{x:m(x)\geq0\ \text{for every }m\in M\}\), and fix a topology \(\tau\) on \(A\). Positivity outside cone closure occurs when there exists \(f\in A\) such that \(f(x)\geq0\) for every \(x\in K_M\) but \(f\notin\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}M\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{Pos}(K_M)\nsubseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}M\). This witnesses failure of the closed certificate cone to represent every polynomial nonnegative on its associated feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This failure occurs when a polynomial is nonnegative on the feasible set but cannot even be approximated, in the chosen topology, by cone certificates.
assumptions_latex: \tau\text{ is a topology on the polynomial space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Pos}(K_M)\nsubseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure condition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no evidence is supplied for the intended topology or the asserted cone-closure representation regime.

children.title: Nonrepresentable Positive Functionals
children.top_down_role: Positive linear functionals lacking compatible representing measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonrepresentable Positive Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of cone positivity to imply representation by a positive measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq A=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a certificate cone. A nonrepresentable \(M\)-positive functional is a linear map \(L:A\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(L(m)\geq0\) for every \(m\in M\), for which no positive Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with all polynomial moments finite satisfies \(L(f)=\int f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in A\). Its existence is exactly a failure of the moment property; if representation specifically by measures supported on \(K_M\) fails, it witnesses failure of the strong moment property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-positive functional is nonrepresentable when it is not integration against any positive measure; its existence defeats the moment property.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq A\text{ is a certificate cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\in M^\vee\setminus\{L_\mu:\mu\text{ is a positive representing measure}\}

notation.meaning: integration functional induced by a measure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polynomial witness that an M-positive functional is not a moment functional on the ambient real space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and let \(L:A\to\mathbb R\) be linear. Then \(L\) has no positive Borel representing measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) with all polynomial moments finite if and only if there exists \(p\in A\) such that \(p\geq0\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(L(p)<0\). In particular, when \(L\) is nonnegative on a certificate cone \(M\), such a \(p\) certifies that the M-positive functional is nonrepresentable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-positive functional is nonrepresentable exactly when it evaluates some globally nonnegative polynomial negatively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{ is nonrepresentable}\iff\exists p\in\operatorname{Pos}(\mathbb R^n):L(p)<0
knowledge_statements.title: Riesz–Haviland Witness for Nonrepresentability

children.title: Duality-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where primal certificate values diverge from dual moment values.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic primal-dual regimes with a strict separation between finite optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\) be a convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\) and \(c\in X\). Define \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in C\}\) and \(d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ y\in Y,\ s\in C^*\}\). Weak duality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\). A positive duality-gap regime occurs when \(p^*,d^*\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(d^*<p^*\). Nonclosedness of an associated feasible-value or projected cone, such as \(\{(Ax,\langle c,x\rangle):x\in C\}\), can obstruct a closedness-based strong-duality argument, although nonclosedness alone does not imply a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive conic duality gap occurs when the finite dual value is strictly below the finite primal value. A nonclosed projected cone may obstruct strong duality but does not alone force a gap.
assumptions_latex: X,Y\text{ are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces}
C\subseteq X\text{ is a convex cone}

notation.meaning: dual cone of C under the inner product on X

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Duality Theory p. 70

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Duality Theory p. 70

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard regularity conditions excluding a finite positive conic duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the finite-dimensional conic primal-dual pair in the accepted seed, assume \(C\) is closed and convex. If the primal has a point \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) with \(Ax=b\) and has finite optimal value, then the dual optimum is attained and \(d^*=p^*\). Symmetrically, if the dual has \(s\in\operatorname{ri}C^*\) satisfying \(A^*y+s=c\) and has finite optimal value, then the primal optimum is attained and \(p^*=d^*\). Thus a finite positive gap is impossible under the applicable Slater condition, while failure of Slater alone does not imply a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-cone Slater regularity excludes a finite positive conic duality gap; failure of Slater is not sufficient to produce one.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed convex cone in finite dimension.
One side is strictly feasible in the appropriate relative interior.
That side has a finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=d^*\text{ and the opposite-side optimum is attained.}

notation.meaning: relative interior of the primal cone
relative interior of the dual cone

children.title: Ordinary Radical Ideals
children.top_down_role: Radicality relative to algebraic varieties without restriction to real points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ring-theoretic radicality without reference to real points or sums of squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a commutative ring and \(I\subseteq A\) an ideal. Define \[\sqrt I:=\{f\in A:f^m\in I\text{ for some integer }m\geq1\}.\] The ideal \(I\) is radical when \(I=\sqrt I\), equivalently when \(f^m\in I\) implies \(f\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ideal is radical when membership of a positive power already implies membership of the element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\text{ is radical}\iff I=\sqrt I.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Membership Definition of Ordinary Radicality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal structural equivalents of ordinary radicality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a commutative ring \(A\) and ideal \(I\subseteq A\), \(I\) is radical if and only if \(A/I\) is reduced. Moreover, \[\sqrt I=\bigcap_{\substack{\mathfrak p\supseteq I\\\mathfrak p\text{ prime}}}\mathfrak p,\] so a radical ideal is exactly an intersection of prime ideals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ideal is radical exactly when its quotient has no nonzero nilpotents, equivalently when it is an intersection of prime ideals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I=\sqrt I\iff A/I\text{ is reduced}\iff I\text{ is an intersection of prime ideals}.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Quotient and Prime-Intersection Characterizations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization of ordinary radicals over an algebraically closed field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be algebraically closed and \(I\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Hilbert's Nullstellensatz gives \[I(V_k(I))=\sqrt I.\] Consequently, \(I\) is radical exactly when it contains every polynomial vanishing on its affine zero set over \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over an algebraically closed field, the vanishing ideal of the zero set of I equals the ordinary radical of I.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(V_k(I))=\sqrt I.

notation.meaning: affine zero set of I over k
ideal vanishing on that zero set

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraically Closed Nullstellensatz Correspondence
Ordinary Radical Ideals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic radicality over a commutative polynomial ring, without restriction to real points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and let \(I\subseteq A\) be an ideal. Its ordinary radical is \(\sqrt{I}=\{f\in A:f^m\in I\text{ for some integer }m\geq1\}\). The ideal \(I\) is radical when \(I=\sqrt{I}\); equivalently, for every \(f\in A\) and \(m\geq1\), the implication \(f^m\in I\Rightarrow f\in I\) holds. This definition is purely ring-theoretic and does not impose conditions involving sums of squares or real solution sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ideal is radical when membership of a positive power of a polynomial already implies membership of the polynomial itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\text{ is radical}\iff I=\sqrt I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordinary-radical definition is standard, precise, and correctly separated from real radicality, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the radical of an ideal and records its basic ideal and affine-variety properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ideal \(I\subseteq k[x]\), its radical is \(\sqrt I:=\{f\in k[x]:f^m\in I\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\}\). The ideal \(I\) is radical when \(I=\sqrt I\). Moreover, \(\sqrt I\) is an ideal, \(V_k(I)=V_k(\sqrt I)\), and the vanishing ideal \(I(V_k(I))\) is radical. When \(k\) is algebraically closed, radical ideals in \(k[x]\) correspond bijectively to affine varieties in \(k^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radical of an ideal consists of the polynomials having some positive power in that ideal. An ideal is radical if it equals its radical. Taking the radical does not change the affine variety, and every vanishing ideal is radical. Over an algebraically closed field, radical ideals and affine varieties correspond bijectively.
assumptions_latex: For the ideal-variety correspondence, \(k\) is algebraically closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt I\) is an ideal, \(V_k(I)=V_k(\sqrt I)\), and \(I(V_k(I))\) is radical; if \(k\) is algebraically closed, radical ideals and affine varieties are in bijection.

children.title: Real Radical Ideals
children.top_down_role: Radicality aligned with real algebraic geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sum-of-Squares Definition of the Real Radical
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-algebraic closure of an ideal characterized by even powers and sums of squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ideal \(I\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), define \[\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}:=\left\{f:\ f^{2m}+\sum_{j=1}^r q_j^2\in I\text{ for some }m\geq1\text{ and }q_j\in\mathbb R[x]\right\}.\] The ideal \(I\) is real radical when \(I=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real radical contains exactly those polynomials whose even power plus a sum of squares belongs to the ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\text{ is real radical}\iff I=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Squares Definition of the Real Radical

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic and real-zero-set properties of real radicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For ideals \(I,J\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \[I\subseteq\sqrt I\subseteq\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I},\qquad I\subseteq J\Rightarrow\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\subseteq\sqrt[\mathbb R]{J},\qquad \sqrt[\mathbb R]{\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}}=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}.\] Moreover, \(V_{\mathbb R}(I)=V_{\mathbb R}(\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Real radicalization is an extensive, monotone, idempotent closure containing ordinary radicalization and preserving the real zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\mapsto\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\text{ is a closure operator and preserves }V_{\mathbb R}(I).
knowledge_statements.title: Real-Radical Closure Laws

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic quotient and prime-intersection characterizations of real radicality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and \(I\subseteq A\). Then \(I\) is real radical if and only if \(A/I\) is real reduced, meaning that \(\sum_{j=1}^r a_j^2=0\) in \(A/I\) implies \(a_j=0\) for every \(j\). Equivalently, \[\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}=\bigcap_{\substack{\mathfrak p\supseteq I\\\mathfrak p\text{ real prime}}}\mathfrak p,\] where \(A/\mathfrak p\) is formally real.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Real radical ideals are exactly those with real-reduced quotients, and the real radical is the intersection of all containing real prime ideals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\iff A/I\text{ is real reduced}.
knowledge_statements.title: Real-Reduced Quotient and Real-Prime Intersection
Real Radical Ideals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radicality characterized by sums of squares and real-algebraic membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and let \(I\subseteq A\) be an ideal. Its real radical is \(\sqrt[\mathrm{r}]{I}=\{f\in A:\text{for some }m\geq1\text{ and }q_1,\ldots,q_r\in A,\ f^{2m}+\sum_{i=1}^r q_i^2\in I\}\). The ideal \(I\) is real radical when \(I=\sqrt[\mathrm{r}]{I}\). Equivalently, whenever \(f^{2m}+\sum_iq_i^2\in I\), one has \(f\in I\). Every real radical ideal is ordinarily radical, while the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real radical ideal absorbs any polynomial whose even power plus a sum of squares belongs to the ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\text{ is real radical}\iff I=\sqrt[\mathrm r]{I}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Real Vanishing Ideal of a Point Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal consisting of all real polynomials that vanish on a specified subset of real affine space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \[I(S):=\{f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]:f(u)=0\text{ for every }u\in S\}.\] Then \(I(S)\) is an ideal and is real radical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real vanishing ideal of a set consists of all real polynomials that vanish at every point of that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(S)\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\text{ is a real radical ideal}.
knowledge_statements.title: Real Vanishing Ideal of a Point Set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-reversing correspondence between real point sets and polynomial ideals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and ideals \(I,J\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \[S\subseteq T\Rightarrow I(T)\subseteq I(S),\qquad I\subseteq J\Rightarrow V_{\mathbb R}(J)\subseteq V_{\mathbb R}(I),\] and \[I\subseteq I(S)\iff S\subseteq V_{\mathbb R}(I).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking real zero sets and taking real vanishing ideals are mutually adjoint order-reversing operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\subseteq I(S)\iff S\subseteq V_{\mathbb R}(I).
knowledge_statements.title: Real Zero-Set–Vanishing-Ideal Galois Connection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure property intrinsic to vanishing ideals of arbitrary real subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its real Zariski closure is \(\overline S^{\mathrm{Zar},\mathbb R}:=V_{\mathbb R}(I(S))\), and \[I(S)=I\!\left(\overline S^{\mathrm{Zar},\mathbb R}\right).\] Consequently, two subsets have the same real vanishing ideal exactly when their real Zariski closures agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real vanishing ideal depends only on the real Zariski closure of its point set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(S)=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I(S))).
knowledge_statements.title: Dependence on Real Zariski Closure
Real Vanishing Ideals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal of all real polynomials vanishing on a prescribed real set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its real vanishing ideal is \(I(S)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]:f(x)=0\text{ for every }x\in S\}\). This is an ideal of \(\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and is real radical. If \(J\) is an ideal and \(V_{\mathbb R}(J)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g(x)=0\text{ for every }g\in J\}\), then \(J\subseteq I(V_{\mathbb R}(J))\); the real Nullstellensatz identifies the latter ideal with \(\sqrt[\mathrm r]{J}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real vanishing ideal consists exactly of polynomials zero at every point of a specified real set; for a real variety it equals the real radical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(V_{\mathbb R}(J))=\sqrt[\mathrm r]{J}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of the real radical with the real vanishing ideal, together with its comparison to the ordinary radical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every ideal \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x]\),
\[
\sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I}=\mathcal I\bigl(V_{\mathbb{R}}(I)\bigr).
\]
Thus \(\sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I}\) is the largest ideal all of whose elements vanish on \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(I)\). Moreover,
\[
I\subseteq\sqrt I\subseteq\sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I},
\]
where \(\sqrt I\) is the ordinary radical of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real radical of an ideal is exactly the ideal of all real polynomials vanishing on its real variety. The original ideal is contained in its ordinary radical, which is contained in its real radical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I}=\mathcal I(V_{\mathbb{R}}(I)),\qquad I\subseteq\sqrt I\subseteq\sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility certificate for polynomial equalities with no common real zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_s\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variety, Real Variety, and Zero-Dimensional Ideal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the complex zero set of an ideal, its generator description and real locus, and the finite-variety criterion for zero-dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an ideal \(\mathcal I\subseteq\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]\), its complex variety is
\[
V(\mathcal I)=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^n:p(\mathbf{x})=0\ \forall p\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
If \(\mathcal I=\langle p_1,\ldots,p_m\rangle\), then
\[
V(\mathcal I)=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^n:p_i(\mathbf{x})=0,
0i=1,
0\ldots,m\}.
\]
The ideal is called zero-dimensional when \(V(\mathcal I)\) is finite, and its real variety is
\[
V^{\mathbb R}(\mathcal I)=V(\mathcal I)\cap\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variety of a polynomial ideal is the set of common complex zeros of all its polynomials; for a generated ideal it is enough to impose the generators. The ideal is zero-dimensional when this complex variety is finite, and its real variety is the subset of real points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(\mathcal I)=\{x\in\mathbb C^n:p(x)=0\ \forall p\in\mathcal I\}=\{x\in\mathbb C^n:p_i(x)=0\ \forall i\},\quad V^{\mathbb R}(\mathcal I)=V(\mathcal I)\cap\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Ideal Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic inclusion from equality generators to all polynomial relations on their real solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\geq 1\), let \(h_1,\ldots,h_m\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and set \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_m\rangle\). Define \(V_{\mathbb R}(I):=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:q(u)=0\text{ for every }q\in I\}\) and, for \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(I(S):=\{p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]:p(u)=0\text{ for every }u\in S\}\). Then every \(p\in I\) vanishes at every \(u\in V_{\mathbb R}(I)\), and consequently \[I\subseteq I(V_{\mathbb R}(I)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polynomial in the ideal generated by the equality constraints vanishes on their common real zero set, so the equality ideal is contained in that set's vanishing ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\subseteq I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Real Radical as a Closure Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality and closure properties of the ideal recovered from a real zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For ideals \(I,J\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the operation \(I\mapsto\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent: \[I\subseteq\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I},\qquad I\subseteq J\Longrightarrow\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\subseteq\sqrt[\mathbb R]{J},\qquad \sqrt[\mathbb R]{\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}}=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}.\] It is the smallest real-radical ideal containing \(I\), and \(V_{\mathbb R}(\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I})=V_{\mathbb R}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Real-radical recovery is a closure operation that preserves the real zero set and produces the smallest real-radical ideal containing the original ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\mapsto\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\) is an extensive, monotone, idempotent closure preserving the real variety.

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Radical Agreement Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equality between supplied relations and all relations visible on the real variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be an ideal. The equality ideal agrees with the full vanishing ideal of its real zero set exactly when it is real radical: \[I=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad I=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}.\] Thus real radicality is precisely the condition under which \(I\) already contains every polynomial relation that vanishes on \(V_{\mathbb R}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality ideal contains every polynomial relation valid on its real zero set if and only if the ideal is real radical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\Longleftrightarrow I=\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Kernel Real-Radical Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact kernel identity for a positive finitely atomic representing measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\in\mathbb R^n\) be distinct, let \(w_1,ldots,w_r>0\), and let \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^r w_i\delta_{u_i}\). For \(p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), set \(L_\mu(p):=\int p\,d\mu\), and define \[\ker M(\mu):=\{p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]:L_\mu(pq)=0\text{ for every }q\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\}.\] If \(S:=\{u_1,\ldots,u_r\}\), then \[\ker M(\mu)=I(S).\] In particular, \(\ker M(\mu)\) is a zero-dimensional real-radical ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive finitely atomic measure, the kernel of its full moment matrix is exactly the real-radical vanishing ideal of its finite support.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker M(\mu)=I(\{u_1,\ldots,u_r\})\), and this ideal is zero-dimensional and real radical.

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Radical Exactness Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates faithful equality modeling from objective-specific finite-order SOS certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,h_1,\ldots,h_m,g_1,\ldots,g_s\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), let \(I:=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_m\rangle\), and let \(K:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_i(x)=0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ g_j(x)\geq0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,s\}\). Assume that \(I\) is real radical and that \(f^*:=\min_{x\in K}f(x)\) exists. For \(d\geq0\), define \[I_{2d}:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i h_i:\phi_i\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\ \deg(\phi_i h_i)\leq2d\right\}\] and \[Q_d(g):=\left\{\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^s\sigma_jg_j:\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_s\text{ are sums of squares},\ \deg(\sigma_0)\leq2d,\ \deg(\sigma_jg_j)\leq2d\right\}.\] Real radicality gives \(I=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\), while membership \[f-f^*\in I_{2d}+Q_d(g)\] is a sufficient order-\(d\) certificate of exactness. Real radicality alone does not imply this finite-degree membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-radical equality ideal faithfully captures all polynomial relations on its real variety, but finite-order SOS exactness needs an additional finite-degree certificate; membership in the truncated ideal plus quadratic module is sufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_i(x)=0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ g_j(x)\geq0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,s\}\) and \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_m\rangle\) is real radical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\), and \(f-f^*\in I_{2d}+Q_d(g)\) is sufficient for an order-\(d\) exactness certificate; real radicality alone does not imply this membership.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper ideal \(I\subset\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the quotient \(A=\mathbb C[x]/I\) is finite-dimensional if and only if, for every \(i\), there is a nonzero \(p_i\in\mathbb C[t]\) with \(p_i(x_i)\in I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A=\mathbb C[x]/I\) is finite-dimensional, multiplication by the coordinate classes defines commuting operators \(M_{x_1},\ldots,M_{x_n}\). Their joint eigenvalue tuples are the points of \(V_{\mathbb C}(I)\), and the associated local generalized eigenspaces encode algebraic multiplicities. If \(I\) is radical, these operators are simultaneously diagonalizable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commuting multiplication matrices have the finite complex variety as their joint spectrum and encode multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_{\mathbb C}(I)\) is the joint spectrum of \((M_{x_1},\ldots,M_{x_n})\), with local-algebra multiplicities.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(S)\) is zero-dimensional and real radical, with \(\dim_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb R[x]/I(S))=|S|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_r\}\), its vanishing ideal satisfies \[I(S)=\bigcap_{i=1}^r\langle x_1-u_{i1},\ldots,x_n-u_{in}\rangle.\] Hence \(I(S)\) is zero-dimensional and real radical, and evaluation induces \[\mathbb R[x]/I(S)\cong\mathbb R^r,\qquad \dim_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb R[x]/I(S))=r.\] The original ideal \(I\) need not equal \(I(S)\) unless it is real radical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite real variety has a zero-dimensional real-radical vanishing ideal whose quotient dimension equals the number of real points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Interpolation on a Finite Real Variety
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate idempotents and representation of functions on a finite real variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_r\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be finite. There exist polynomials \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\in\mathbb R[x]\) with \(e_i(u_j)=\delta_{ij}\). Consequently every function \(a:S\to\mathbb R\) is represented on \(S\) by \(p=\sum_{i=1}^r a(u_i)e_i\), and in \(\mathbb R[x]/I(S)\) one has \([e_i][e_j]=\delta_{ij}[e_i]\) and \(\sum_i[e_i]=[1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real-valued function on a finite real variety has a polynomial representative, with idempotent polynomials selecting the individual points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R[x]/I(S)\cong\mathbb R^r\) has coordinate idempotents, and every function \(S\to\mathbb R\) has a polynomial representative.

Then near \(u\), \(h^{-1}(0)\) is a smooth submanifold of dimension \(n-m\geq1\), hence contains infinitely many points and a nonconstant smooth local curve through \(u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complex Dimension Does Not Determine Real-Locus Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates positive complex dimension from positive semialgebraic dimension of the real locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(I=\langle x^2+y^2\rangle\subset\mathbb R[x,y]\), \(V_{\mathbb C}(I)\) has complex dimension one, whereas \(V_{\mathbb R}(I)=\{(0,0)\}\) has semialgebraic dimension zero. Thus positive complex dimension does not imply a positive-dimensional real locus.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Semialgebraic Dimension of a Real Variety
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic real-locus dimension convention for distinguishing continua from finite real varieties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ideal I\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n], give V_{\mathbb R}(I) its semialgebraic dimension. For any finite semialgebraic C^1 stratification V_{\mathbb R}(I)=\bigsqcup_\alpha S_\alpha, one has \dim V_{\mathbb R}(I)=\max_\alpha\dim S_\alpha. Hence \dim V_{\mathbb R}(I)\ge1 exactly when some stratum has positive dimension; equivalently, the real locus contains a nonconstant semialgebraic arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real variety is positive-dimensional when its real locus has positive semialgebraic dimension, equivalently when a semialgebraic stratification has a positive-dimensional stratum or the locus contains a nonconstant semialgebraic arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim V_{\mathbb R}(I)\ge1\iff\text{some semialgebraic stratum has positive dimension}\iff V_{\mathbb R}(I)\text{ contains a nonconstant semialgebraic arc}.

Such a variety is infinite and contains a nonconstant semialgebraic curve locally on some stratum; it cannot be represented by a finite support alone.

Then \(V_{\mathbb R}(I)=\mathbb R\), whereas \[K=V_{\mathbb R}(I)\cap\{x\geq0,-x\geq0\}=\{0\}.\] Hence \(I(K)=\langle x\rangle\) is zero-dimensional and real radical while \(I=(0)\subsetneq I(K)\).

children.title: Nonradical Multiplicity
children.top_down_role: Repeated algebraic structure retained by the generated ideal.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ideal \(\langle x^m\rangle\) retains multiplicity and is strictly smaller than its real vanishing ideal for every \(m\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical univariate model of multiplicity invisible to the underlying real zero set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any integer \(m\geq2\), let \(I_m=\langle x^m\rangle\subset\mathbb R[x]\). Then \[V_{\mathbb R}(I_m)=\{0\},\qquad I(V_{\mathbb R}(I_m))=\langle x\rangle,\qquad I_m\subsetneq\langle x\rangle.\] In the quotient \(\mathbb R[x]/I_m\), the nonzero residue class \(\bar x\) is nilpotent because \(\bar x^m=0\). The equality ideal therefore retains multiplicity that is absent from its real point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ideal generated by a repeated factor retains nilpotent multiplicity, although its real zero set is unchanged after removing that multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic characterization of the repeated algebraic structure retained by a nonradical ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and let \(I\subseteq A\) be an ideal. Then \(I\) is nonradical if and only if \(A/I\) contains a nonzero nilpotent element. Explicitly, \(f+I\neq0\) and \((f+I)^m=0\) for some \(m\geq1\) exactly when \(f\notin I\) and \(f^m\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ideal retains nonradical multiplicity exactly when its quotient ring contains a nonzero nilpotent residue class.
assumptions_latex: \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is a polynomial ring over a field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\neq\sqrt I\iff A/I\text{ contains a nonzero nilpotent element}.

knowledge_statements.title: Radical but Non-Real-Radical Ideals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard example separating ordinary radicality from real radicality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I:=\langle x^2+y^2\rangle\subseteq\mathbb R[x,y]\). The polynomial \(x^2+y^2\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb R[x,y]\), and \(I\) is prime and therefore radical. Its real zero set and real vanishing ideal are \[V_{\mathbb R}(I)=\{(0,0)\},\qquad I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))=\langle x,y\rangle.\] Consequently, \[I=\sqrt I\subsetneq\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}=\langle x,y\rangle.\] Thus ordinary radicality over \(\mathbb R[x,y]\) does not imply real radicality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ideal generated by x squared plus y squared is radical over the real polynomial ring, but its real vanishing ideal is strictly larger, so it is not real radical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x^2+y^2\rangle\) is radical but not real radical.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in V\), define the intrinsic Zariski tangent space by \[T_xV=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\nabla p(x)^{\mathsf T}v=0\text{ for every }p\in I(V)\}.\] The point \(x\) is singular when \(\dim_{\mathbb{R}}T_xV>d_x\), where \(d_x\) is the local real-algebraic dimension of \(V\) at \(x\); otherwise it is regular.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian-Minor Description of the Equidimensional Singular Locus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-based singular-locus test under hypotheses ensuring a uniform expected codimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(I(V)=\langle f_1,\ldots,f_s\rangle\subseteq\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and that the intrinsic reduced variety is equidimensional of dimension \(d\). Let \(J_f=(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)\). Then its real singular locus is \[\operatorname{Sing}_{\mathbb R}(V)=V_{\mathbb R}\!\left(I(V)+I_{n-d}(J_f)\right),\] where \(I_{n-d}(J_f)\) is generated by all \((n-d)\)-minors of \(J_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an equidimensional intrinsic real variety, adjoining the relevant Jacobian minors cuts out its real singular locus.
assumptions_latex: \(I(V)\) is the full real vanishing ideal and is generated by \(f_1,\ldots,f_s\).
The associated reduced variety is equidimensional of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Sing}_{\mathbb R}(V)=V_{\mathbb R}(I(V)+I_{n-d}(J_f)).

notation.meaning: ideal generated by the minors of size n-d

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced Cusp with a Singular Real Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates intrinsic singularity from nonradical multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=V_{\mathbb R}(y^2-x^3)\subseteq\mathbb R^2\). Its real vanishing ideal is \(I(V)=\langle y^2-x^3\rangle\), which is prime and hence radical. The local dimension at \((0,0)\) is one, while \(\nabla(y^2-x^3)(0,0)=0\), so \(T_{(0,0)}V=\mathbb R^2\). Thus \((0,0)\) is singular although the coordinate ring is reduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real cusp is singular at the origin even though its vanishing ideal is radical.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Cusp with a Singular Real Point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic local-algebra equivalent of the tangent-space definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z\in\operatorname{relint}(K)\), set \(L=\operatorname{aff}(K)-z\), and suppose \(f\) is twice differentiable near \(z\), \(f\geq0\) on \(K\), and \(f(z)=0\). Then \(
abla f(z)^{\mathsf T}v=0\) and \(v^{\mathsf T}
abla^2f(z)v\geq0\) for every \(v\in L\). If \(

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{aff}(K)-z\), and let \(M\subseteq\operatorname{relint}(K)\) be a positive-dimensional \(C^2\) submanifold relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(K)\). Suppose \(f\) is twice differentiable, \(f\geq0\) on \(K\) near \(M\), and \(f|_M=0\). For every \(z\in M\), the projection of \(\nabla f(z)\) onto \(L\) is zero, and the Hessian restricted to \(L\) annihilates every \(v\in T_zM\). Hence the affine-hull Hessian cannot be positive definite.

This condition records objective flatness along feasible approaches and does not require the local constraint scheme itself to be nonreduced.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_z\) be the common kernel of the equality and active-inequality gradients, and let \(L\) be the associated first-order Lagrangian. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Hessian Condition Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to interpreting failure of the boundary Hessian condition as nonmembership in the quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=[-1,1]=\{x:1-x^2\geq0\}\) and \(M=M(1-x^2)\). For every integer \(m\geq2\), the polynomial \(f(x)=x^{2m}\) belongs to \(M\), since it is a square, but at its interior zero \(x=0\) its quadratic local term vanishes, so the boundary Hessian condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact certificate membership can hold even when the boundary Hessian condition fails; even powers of degree at least four on an interval give a canonical family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in M\quad\text{and}\quad f\text{ does not satisfy the boundary Hessian condition at }0.\)

notation.meaning: quadratic module generated by the interval constraint

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Hessian Condition Is Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global quadratic-module membership under the boundary Hessian condition at every feasible zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and suppose the quadratic module \(M(g)\) is Archimedean. If \(f\geq0\) on \(K\) and \(f\) satisfies the boundary Hessian condition at every \(u\in K\) with \(f(u)=0\), then \(f\in M(g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an Archimedean quadratic module, boundary-Hessian regularity at every feasible zero upgrades nonnegativity to exact quadratic-module membership.
assumptions_latex: The boundary Hessian condition holds at every \(u\in Z_K(f)\).

notation.meaning: quadratic module generated by the inequality polynomials
zero set of f in K

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Hessian Membership Theorem
Boundary Hessian Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marshall’s local boundary Hessian condition at a zero of a polynomial on a basic closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(u\in K\) be a nonsingular point, and suppose regular local parameters \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) satisfy \(K=\{t_1\geq0,\ldots,t_k\geq0\}\) locally at \(u\). Write the formal local expansion as \(f=f(u)+f_1+f_2+\cdots\), where \(f_j\) is homogeneous of degree \(j\) in the parameters. The boundary Hessian condition holds at \(u\) when \(f(u)=0\), \(f_1=a_1t_1+\cdots+a_kt_k\) with \(a_i>0\), and the quadratic form \(f_2(0,\ldots,0,t_{k+1},\ldots,t_n)\) is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular boundary zero, the active inward linear coefficients must be positive and the quadratic term along unconstrained tangent directions must be positive definite.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) is nonsingular and admits the stated regular parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_i>0\) for \(1\leq i\leq k\), and \(f_2|_{t_1=\cdots=t_k=0}\) is positive definite.

notation.meaning: regular local parameters at the zero
degree-j homogeneous term of the local expansion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but its exact local-parameter formulation requires an authoritative definition or theorem locator.

children.title: Local–Global Degeneracy Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Degeneracy Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of local–global criteria requiring isolated zeros or nondegenerate local boundary data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=[-1,1]^2\) and \(f(x,y)=x^2y^2\). Then \(f\geq0\) on \(K\), but its zero set is \(\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\}\), hence is nonisolated. At the interior zero \((0,0)\), both the linear and quadratic terms vanish, so the interior specialization of the boundary Hessian condition fails. Consequently, a local–global theorem whose hypotheses require finitely many zeros and the boundary Hessian condition cannot be invoked. This failure does not imply nonmembership in a positivity cone: here \(f=(xy)^2\) is itself a sum of squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonisolated or degenerate zeros block isolated-zero local–global criteria, although the polynomial may still possess a positivity certificate by another argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_K(f)\) is nonisolated and the local nondegeneracy hypothesis fails, while \(f\in\Sigma[x,y]\).

notation.meaning: zero set of f within K
cone of sums of squares in the polynomial ring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly illustrates nonisolated, degenerate zeros and does not overclaim nonmembership, but the stated local–global hypothesis boundary lacks a source locator.

children.title: Krivine–Stengle Strict-Positivity Regime
children.top_down_role: General semialgebraic strict-positivity applicability.

knowledge_statements.title: Krivine–Stengle Strict-Positivity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-positivity form of the Krivine–Stengle Positivstellensatz with inequalities and equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m;\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\). Let \(T(g)\) be the preordering generated by \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\), and let \(I(h)\) be the ideal generated by \(h_1,\ldots,h_r\). For \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\), strict positivity \(f>0\) on \(K\) is equivalent to the existence of \(s,t\in T(g)\) and \(q\in I(h)\) satisfying \(sf=1+t+q\). Evaluating this identity at any feasible point directly verifies strict positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is strictly positive on a basic semialgebraic set exactly when a preordering multiplier converts it to one plus another preordering element, modulo equations.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the displayed basic semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f>0\text{ on }K\iff \exists s,t\in T(g),\ q\in I(h):\ sf=1+t+q\).

notation.meaning: preordering generated by the inequality polynomials
ideal generated by the equality polynomials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate has the expected strict-positivity form and fits the leaf, but no source supports the precise equivalence; the final evaluation sentence is also proof text.

children.title: Krivine–Stengle Nonnegativity Regime
children.top_down_role: General semialgebraic nonnegativity applicability including zeros.

knowledge_statements.title: Krivine–Stengle Nonnegativity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegativity form allowing zeros through an even-power correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the basic semialgebraic set \(K\), preordering \(T(g)\), and equality ideal \(I(h)\) defined in the strict-positivity regime, a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\) is nonnegative on \(K\) if and only if there exist an integer \(N\geq0\), elements \(s,t\in T(g)\), and \(q\in I(h)\) such that \(sf=f^{2N}+t+q\). The even-power term permits zeros of \(f\); at every feasible point the identity rules out \(f<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegativity, including zeros, is characterized by a preordering multiplier identity containing an even power of the polynomial and the equality ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\geq0\text{ on }K\iff \exists N\geq0,\ s,t\in T(g),\ q\in I(h):\ sf=f^{2N}+t+q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The even-power nonnegativity certificate is plausible, but the exact exponent and preordering formulation require a theorem locator; the explanatory final sentence is proof text.

children.title: Krivine–Stengle Vanishing Regime
children.top_down_role: General semialgebraic applicability for polynomials vanishing throughout the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Krivine–Stengle Vanishing Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-radical certificate for a polynomial vanishing throughout a basic semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\{g_i\geq0,\ h_j=0\}\), let \(T(g)\) denote the generated preordering and \(I(h)\) the equality ideal. A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\) vanishes at every point of \(K\) if and only if there exist an integer \(N\geq1\), an element \(t\in T(g)\), and an element \(q\in I(h)\) such that \(f^{2N}+t+q=0\). At feasible points, both \(f^{2N}\) and \(t\) are nonnegative, so the identity is directly checkable as a vanishing certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing on the feasible set is equivalent to an even power plus a preordering element belonging to the negative equality ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_K=0\iff \exists N\geq1,\ t\in T(g),\ q\in I(h):\ f^{2N}+t+q=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vanishing certificate fits the terminal container, but its precise real-radical equivalence requires an authoritative locator; the feasible-point argument is proof text.

children.title: Krivine–Stengle Infeasibility Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Krivine–Stengle Infeasibility Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General preordering certificate for emptiness of a basic semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m;\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\), with generated preordering \(T(g)\) and ideal \(I(h)\). Then \(K=\varnothing\) if and only if there exist \(t\in T(g)\) and \(q\in I(h)\) satisfying \(-1=t+q\). Indeed, evaluation at a feasible point would make \(t\geq0\) and \(q=0\), contradicting \(-1\geq0\); the Positivstellensatz supplies the converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic semialgebraic set is empty exactly when minus one belongs to its inequality preordering plus its equality ideal.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the displayed basic semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\varnothing\iff -1\in T(g)+I(h)\).

notation.meaning: preordering generated by the inequality polynomials
ideal generated by the equality polynomials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The infeasibility identity is standard and appropriately classified as a certificate, but the equivalence has no cited source and the statement includes proof text.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Certificate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of complete preordering and Archimedean quadratic-module emptiness certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\{g_i\geq0,\ h_j=0\}\), the identity \(-1=t+q\), with \(t\in T(g)\) and \(q\in I(h)\), is a complete infeasibility certificate without compactness assumptions. If the smaller quadratic module \(M(g)+I(h)\) is Archimedean, emptiness also implies \(-1\in M(g)+I(h)\), by applying the Archimedean strict-positivity theorem to the vacuously positive polynomial \(-1\). In either regime, displaying the polynomial identity certifies \(K=\varnothing\) by evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preorderings give general emptiness certificates; an Archimedean quadratic module gives the smaller module certificate under its additional boundedness assumption.
assumptions_latex: For the quadratic-module conclusion, \(M(g)+I(h)\) is Archimedean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\varnothing\Rightarrow -1\in T(g)+I(h)\), and under Archimedeanity \(K=\varnothing\Rightarrow -1\in M(g)+I(h)\).

notation.meaning: quadratic module generated by the inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison of complete preordering and Archimedean quadratic-module regimes is plausible, but both implications need specific theorem locators and the statement includes derivational text.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Set Detection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical limits of restricted-cone and degree-truncated infeasibility searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\) be a sound certificate cone for \(K\), and let \(C_d\) be its degree-\(2d\) truncation. Membership \(-1\in C_d+I(h)\) certifies \(K=\varnothing\). Conversely, failure of this finite search, \(-1\notin C_d+I(h)\), establishes only that no certificate of the prescribed cone and degree exists. It does not imply \(K\neq\varnothing\). Such a converse requires both completeness of the untruncated cone and an applicable degree bound; replacing the full preordering by a non-Archimedean quadratic module may also destroy completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding minus one proves emptiness, but failure at a fixed degree or in an incomplete cone does not prove feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(C_d\subseteq C\) is the degree-truncated certificate cone.
Every element of \(C+I(h)\) is nonnegative on \(K\).

\(-1\in C_d+I(h)\Rightarrow K=\varnothing\), whereas \(-1
otin C_d+I(h)
ot\Rightarrow K
eq\varnothing\).

children.title: Haviland Representation Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Haviland Representation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-sensitive characterization of full moment functionals by positivity on all polynomials nonnegative on the support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(L:\mathbb R[x]\to\mathbb R\) be linear. There exists a positive Borel measure \(\mu\) supported on \(K\), finite on every polynomial moment, such that \(L(p)=\int_K p\,d\mu\) for every \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\), if and only if \(L(p)\geq0\) for every polynomial \(p\) satisfying \(p(x)\geq0\) for all \(x\in K\). Thus the exact dual cone is the cone of all polynomials nonnegative on \(K\), not merely a selected sums-of-squares cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear polynomial functional has a measure supported on a closed set exactly when it is nonnegative on every polynomial nonnegative there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(p)=\int_Kp\,d\mu\ \forall p\iff L(q)\geq0\ \forall q\geq0\text{ on }K\).

notation.meaning: linear functional on the polynomial ring
positive Borel representing measure supported on K

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation statement matches Haviland's theorem and the leaf role, but no inspectable theorem or section locator is supplied.
