children.title: Gröbner-Basis Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Symbolic interfaces for equality-ideal dimension and quotient structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite quotient structure following a zero-dimensional diagnosis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A=k[x]/I\) is finite-dimensional with quotient basis \(\mathcal B\), multiplication by \([x_i]\) defines commuting matrices \(M_{x_i}\), and multiplication by \([f]\) is \(f(M_{x_1},\ldots,M_{x_n})\). Over an algebraic closure, the joint eigenvalue tuples of the coordinate multiplication matrices are the points of \(V(I)\); their generalized joint eigenspaces encode local quotient lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite polynomial quotient is represented by commuting coordinate multiplication matrices whose joint spectrum gives its algebraic solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_f=f(M_{x_1},\ldots,M_{x_n})\text{, and the joint spectrum encodes }V(I).

notation.meaning: matrix of multiplication by the coordinate class

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplication-Matrix Quotient Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent initial-ideal test for zero-dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subsetneq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and let \(G\) be a Gröbner basis for a fixed monomial order. Then \(I\) is zero-dimensional if and only if, for every \(i\), some positive power \(x_i^{m_i}\) belongs to \(\operatorname{in}(I)\); equivalently, a leading monomial in \(G\) divides a positive pure power of each variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ideal is zero-dimensional exactly when its initial ideal contains a positive pure power of every variable.
assumptions_latex: A monomial order and Gröbner basis are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(k[x]/I)=0\iff\forall i\ \exists m_i\ge1:\ x_i^{m_i}\in\operatorname{in}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Power Zero-Dimensionality Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_s\rangle\subsetneq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is a proper finitely generated ideal over a field \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is zero-dimensional if and only if \(\mathcal{B}\) is finite; then the residue classes of \(\mathcal{B}\) form a \(k\)-basis of \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\).

notation.meaning: leading monomial of a basis polynomial

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnose equality-ideal dimension through leading monomials and quotient-basis finiteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I=\langle h_1,\ldots,h_s\rangle\subsetneq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a proper ideal, where \(k\) is a field, and fix a monomial order. Compute a Gröbner basis \(G\) of \(I\) and the standard monomials
\[
\mathcal{B}=\{x^\alpha:\operatorname{LM}(g)\nmid x^\alpha\text{ for every }g\in G\}.
\]
The diagnostic declares \(I\) zero-dimensional exactly when \(\mathcal{B}\) is finite. In that case, the residue classes of \(\mathcal{B}\) form a \(k\)-basis of \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\), and \(|\mathcal{B}|=\dim_k(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper ideal, compute a Gröbner basis and its standard monomials; their finiteness exactly diagnoses zero-dimensionality and supplies a quotient-space basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Gröbner-Basis Diagnostics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gröbner Bases and Reduced Gröbner Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a Gröbner basis, states uniqueness of the reduced basis, and records Buchberger's construction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq k[x]\) be an ideal and fix a term order \(\succ\). A finite set \(G_\succ=\{g_1,\ldots,g_t\}\subseteq I\) is a Gröbner basis of \(I\) when \(\langle\operatorname{in}_\succ(g_1),\ldots,\operatorname{in}_\succ(g_t)\rangle=\operatorname{in}_\succ(I)\). For each fixed term order, \(I\) has a unique reduced Gröbner basis, and Buchberger's algorithm computes a Gröbner basis from generators of \(I\) and the chosen order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gröbner basis is a finite subset of an ideal whose initial terms generate the ideal's initial ideal. Every fixed term order determines a unique reduced Gröbner basis, and Buchberger's algorithm computes a Gröbner basis from ideal generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\succ\) is a Gröbner basis iff \(\langle\operatorname{in}_\succ(g_1),\ldots,\operatorname{in}_\succ(g_t)\rangle=\operatorname{in}_\succ(I)\); the reduced Gröbner basis for \(\succ\) is unique.

children.title: Resultant-Based Finiteness Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Resultant interfaces for detecting finite algebraic solution structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bézout Length under a Nonvanishing Leading Resultant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative affine finiteness consequence with algebraic multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_1,\ldots,h_n\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have degrees \(d_1,\ldots,d_n>0\), and suppose \(\operatorname{Res}(h_1^{\mathrm{top}},\ldots,h_n^{\mathrm{top}})\ne0\). Then the homogenized equations have no common point at infinity and define a zero-dimensional complete intersection. Consequently \[\dim_k k[x]/\langle h_1,\ldots,h_n\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^n d_i.\] Thus the affine zero set is finite, possibly empty only if the quotient is the zero ring, and its number of distinct points is at most \(\prod_i d_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero resultant of the leading forms certifies affine finiteness and gives the Bézout length counted with multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: There are n positive-degree polynomials in n variables.
The resultant of their leading homogeneous parts is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_k k[x]/\langle h_1,\ldots,h_n\rangle=\prod_i d_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bézout Length under a Nonvanishing Leading Resultant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defining projective property of the multivariate homogeneous resultant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_1,\ldots,F_n\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be positive-degree homogeneous forms over an algebraically closed field. Then \[\operatorname{Res}(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=0\iff\exists [x]\in\mathbb P_k^{n-1}:F_1(x)=\cdots=F_n(x)=0.\] The universal resultant is multihomogeneous of degree \(\prod_{j\ne i}\deg F_j\) in the coefficients of \(F_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The homogeneous resultant vanishes exactly when the forms have a common projective zero.
assumptions_latex: There are n positive-degree homogeneous forms in n variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Res}(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=0\iff V_+(F_1,\ldots,F_n)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Resultant Vanishing Criterion
Resultant-Based Finiteness Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonvanishing resultant of leading forms excludes solutions at infinity and ensures finite intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h_1,\ldots,h_n\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have positive degrees, with \(k\) algebraically closed, and let \(h_i^{\mathrm{top}}\) denote the highest-degree homogeneous part of \(h_i\). If
\[
\operatorname{Res}(h_1^{\mathrm{top}},\ldots,h_n^{\mathrm{top}})\ne0,
\]
then the leading forms have no common point in projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}_k\). Consequently, the affine common-zero set \(V(h_1,\ldots,h_n)\subset k^n\) has no positive-dimensional component and is finite, possibly empty. Vanishing of the resultant is only an exceptional-locus warning and does not alone prove infinitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero resultant of the leading homogeneous forms excludes common directions at infinity and certifies that the square affine system has finitely many solutions.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) positive-degree polynomials in \(n\) variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonvanishing of \(\operatorname{Res}(h_1^{\mathrm{top}},\ldots,h_n^{\mathrm{top}})\) implies that \(V(h_1,\ldots,h_n)\) is finite.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a square system over an algebraically closed field, nonvanishing of the homogeneous resultant of the leading forms does exclude projective solutions at infinity and implies a finite affine zero set. The condition content kind fits, but no elimination-theory source is supplied.

children.title: Discriminant-Based Singularity Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Discriminant interfaces for locating singular or degenerate data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric discriminant for the smooth part of a generically finite morphism; nonproperness and singular total-space effects remain separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:X\to P\) be a dominant generically finite morphism of varieties over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. On \(X_{\mathrm{sm}}\), set \(C_\pi=\{x:\operatorname{rank}(d\pi_x)<\dim P\}\). The critical-value discriminant is \(\Delta_\pi=\overline{\pi(C_\pi)}\). Thus \(P\setminus\Delta_\pi\) contains no critical value arising from \(X_{\mathrm{sm}}\); this definition alone does not exclude nonproper fibers or effects from singular points of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical-value discriminant is the closure of critical values of the smooth part of a generically finite map.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:X\to P\) is dominant and generically finite.
The base field is algebraically closed of characteristic zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_\pi=\overline{\pi(C_\pi)}\), with nonproperness and singular-source effects requiring separate loci.

notation.meaning: critical locus on the smooth part of X

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Value Discriminant Locus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact repeated-root diagnostic for a univariate polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(T)=a_d\prod_{i=1}^d(T-r_i)\in k[T]\) over a characteristic-zero field, \[\operatorname{Disc}(f)=a_d^{2d-2}\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2=(-1)^{d(d-1)/2}a_d^{-1}\operatorname{Res}(f,f').\] Hence \(\operatorname{Disc}(f)=0\) if and only if \(f\) has a multiple root over an algebraic closure, equivalently \(\gcd(f,f')\ne1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A univariate polynomial has zero discriminant exactly when it has a repeated root.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has positive degree and nonzero leading coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Disc}(f)=0\iff f\text{ has a multiple root}\iff\gcd(f,f')\ne1\).

notation.meaning: resultant of f and its derivative

knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Discriminant Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Jacobian Elimination Misses Escape to Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of an affine equation-plus-Jacobian diagnostic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x;p)=px-1\), every fiber with \(p\ne0\) consists of the nonsingular point \(x=p^{-1}\), whereas the fiber at \(p=0\) is empty and the solution escapes to infinity as \(p\to0\). Since \(\partial h/\partial x=p\) and \(\langle px-1,p\rangle=\langle1\rangle\), eliminating \(x\) from the affine equation and its Jacobian detects no exceptional parameter. Thus affine Jacobian elimination alone does not detect this nonproper degeneration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family px−1 has an escaping solution at p=0 that affine equation-plus-Jacobian elimination misses.
assumptions_latex: The family is considered in affine \(x\)-space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=0\text{ is a nonproperness value not detected by }\langle h,\partial h/\partial x\rangle\cap k[p].
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Jacobian Elimination Misses Escape to Infinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precise multivariate criterion requiring properness, flatness, and absence of ramification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:X\to P\) be a dominant generically finite morphism of finite type over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let \(U\subseteq P\) be a dense open set such that \(\pi_U:X\times_PU\to U\) is proper, flat, and unramified. Then \(\pi_U\) is finite étale. On each connected component of \(U\), every geometric fiber is reduced and has constant cardinality equal to the generic degree of \(\pi\). Consequently, a discriminant complement certifying constant nonsingular finite fibers must exclude nonproperness, nonflatness, and ramification values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper, flat, unramified restriction of a generically finite family is finite étale and has reduced constant-cardinality fibers.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:X\to P\) is dominant, generically finite, and of finite type.
The base field is algebraically closed of characteristic zero.
Over \(U\), the morphism is proper, flat, and unramified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_U\text{ is finite étale, with fiber cardinality }\deg(\pi)\text{ on each connected component of }U.

notation.meaning: open complement of the complete exceptional locus
restriction of the family over U

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Étale Discriminant Complement
Discriminant-Based Singularity Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A discriminant polynomial identifies parameter values where a generically finite system becomes singular or degenerates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h_1(x;p),\ldots,h_n(x;p)\in k[x,p]\) be a parameterized square system over a characteristic-zero algebraically closed field. Assume its generic fiber is a finite complete intersection with no solutions at infinity. Let \(\Delta(p)\) be an elimination polynomial obtained from the homogenized equations together with
\[
J(x;p)=\det\!\left(\frac{\partial h_i}{\partial x_j}(x;p)\right).
\]
For any parameter \(p_0\) with \(\Delta(p_0)\ne0\), the fiber is finite, retains the generic degree, and every solution has \(J(x;p_0)\ne0\). Hence all its solutions are isolated and nonsingular; \(\Delta(p_0)=0\) marks a possible singularity, degree drop, or solution at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the discriminant locus, a generically finite square polynomial system retains its degree and has only isolated nonsingular solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is algebraically closed of characteristic zero.
The generic fiber is a finite complete intersection without solutions at infinity.
\(\Delta\) eliminates the equations and their Jacobian determinant, including projective degeneracies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta(p_0)\ne0\) implies that the fiber at \(p_0\) is finite and every solution is nonsingular.

notation.meaning: Jacobian determinant with respect to the unknowns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The phrase 'an elimination polynomial' does not uniquely guarantee detection of every singular fiber, degree drop, and projective degeneration. A precise discriminant construction and authoritative source are required before the nonvanishing conclusion and generic-degree claim can be assessed reliably.

children.title: Exceptional-Parameter Loci
children.top_down_role: Parameter subsets associated with changes in finiteness or regularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact constructible stratification replacing reliance on one incompletely specified diagnostic polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A comprehensive Gröbner system for \(I\subset k[p,x]\) is a finite collection \(\{(S_i,G_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) of constructible parameter strata covering \(\bar k^s\) such that, for every \(a\in S_i\), \(G_i(a)\) is a Gröbner basis of the specialized ideal \(I_a\) with the prescribed leading-monomial pattern. Consequently standard-monomial finiteness and quotient dimension are constant on each stratum with a fixed initial ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comprehensive Gröbner system partitions parameter space into constructible strata carrying valid specialized Gröbner data.
assumptions_latex: A monomial order in the unknown variables is fixed.
The comprehensive Gröbner system is computed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_iS_i=\bar k^s\) and \(a\in S_i\Rightarrow G_i(a)\text{ is a Gröbner basis of }I_a\).
knowledge_statements.title: Comprehensive Gröbner Stratification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Constancy of the Projective Hilbert Polynomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic exceptional closed subset for a projective family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:X\to P\) be a projective morphism of finite type with \(P\) integral. There is a nonempty Zariski-open subset \(U\subseteq P\) on which \(\pi\) is flat. Relative to a fixed relatively ample line bundle, the Hilbert polynomial of \(X_p\) is constant on \(U\). Hence fiber dimension and projective degree can change only in the proper closed subset \(P\setminus U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projective algebraic family has constant fiber Hilbert polynomial, dimension, and degree on a dense open parameter set.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:X\to P\) is projective and of finite type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\,\varnothing\ne U\subseteq P\text{ open such that }\operatorname{Hilb}(X_p)\text{ is constant on }U\).
knowledge_statements.title: Generic Constancy of the Projective Hilbert Polynomial

assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a characteristic-zero field and \(I\subset k[p_1,\ldots,p_s,x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is an ideal.
A block term order eliminates the variables \(x\), and \(G\) is a Gröbner basis of \(I k(p)[x]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\notin E_G\) guarantees that every coefficient of \(G\) specializes and that the specialized leading monomials agree with the generic ones.

notation.meaning: Product of the cleared denominators and leading coefficients occurring in the generic Gröbner basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-dependent exceptional locus for generic elimination under parameter specialization.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Clear all parameter denominators in \(G\), and let \(D_G(p)\) be the product of those denominators and the resulting leading coefficients. The Gröbner exceptional-parameter locus is
\[
E_G:=V(D_G)\subseteq\overline{k}^{s}.
\]
For every \(a\notin E_G\), specialization \(p\mapsto a\) preserves the defined coefficients and leading monomials of \(G\); hence the generic elimination computation specializes without the coefficient or leading-term failures detected by \(D_G\). Points of \(E_G\) are candidates for changed fiber dimension, degree, or multiplicity, but membership in \(E_G\) alone does not prove that such a change occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exceptional locus is the parameter zero set where denominators or leading coefficients used by a generic elimination computation vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Exceptional-Parameter Loci

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited elementary-algebraic-geometry locator does not substantiate the parameter-specialization claim. Avoiding only denominators and leading coefficients appearing in G need not preserve the Gröbner-basis computation; denominators or coefficients used in Buchberger reductions and representations may also need exclusion. The plain statement also omits the specialization guarantee and caveat.

children.title: Elimination Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where resultant or discriminant information is insufficient for the intended diagnosis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between a parameter projection and the variety of its elimination ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(I\subset k[p,x]\) over an algebraically closed field, \(V(I\cap k[p])=\overline{\pi_p(V(I))}\). For \(I=\langle px-1\rangle\), one has \(I\cap k[p]=(0)\) but \(\pi_p(V(I))=k\setminus\{0\}\). Thus \(p=0\) satisfies every elimination equation although its fiber is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elimination describes the Zariski closure of a projection and can include parameters absent from the projection itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(I\cap k[p])=\overline{\pi_p(V(I))}\), while equality with \(\pi_p(V(I))\) can fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Error in Elimination

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by components excluded from the intended affine or residual geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a homogenized ideal and let \(B\) define an extraneous locus, such as a base locus or the irrelevant locus. Raw elimination from \(I\) can retain conditions contributed only by components contained in \(V(B)\). The residual geometry is represented by \(I:B^\infty=\{f:\exists m,\ fB^m\subseteq I\}\). A diagnostic computed without the required saturation can therefore vanish because of an excluded component and is inconclusive for the intended fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw projective elimination can retain excluded components; the appropriate residual ideal is obtained by saturation.
assumptions_latex: The locus \(V(B)\) is extraneous to the intended solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual elimination problem is based on \(I:B^\infty\), not generally on \(I\).

notation.meaning: saturation of I by the ideal B

knowledge_statements.title: Saturation Boundary for Projective Elimination

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient certificate for specialization of a fixed generic Gröbner computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\langle f_1,\ldots,f_s\rangle\subset k[p][x]\), and let \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_t\}\subset k(p)[x]\). Record identities proving \(G\subset Ik(p)[x]\), \(I\subset\langle G\rangle\), and the reduction to zero of every Buchberger \(S\)-polynomial of \(G\). Let \(D(p)\) be the product of every denominator appearing in these identities and reductions and every coefficient whose nonvanishing preserves a leading monomial. If \(D(a)\ne0\), all recorded identities specialize, \(G(a)\) generates \(I_a\), its leading monomials are preserved, and Buchberger's criterion shows that \(G(a)\) is a Gröbner basis of \(I_a\) with the same initial ideal. If \(D(a)=0\), this fixed trace is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete algebraic trace of membership identities, protected leading coefficients, and Buchberger reductions certifies Gröbner specialization wherever all recorded factors remain nonzero.
assumptions_latex: A fixed monomial order is used.
The complete membership and Buchberger-reduction trace is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(a)\text{ is a Gröbner basis of }I_a\text{ and }\operatorname{in}(I_a)=\langle\operatorname{LM}(G)\rangle.

notation.meaning: product of trace denominators and protected leading coefficients

knowledge_statements.title: Trace-Verified Gröbner Specialization Certificate

assumptions_latex: The parameterized ideal and generic Gröbner computation satisfy the assumptions of the exceptional-locus record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(D_G(a)\ne0\), the listed specialization failures are excluded; if \(D_G(a)=0\), the generic elimination certificate is inconclusive and recomputation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of validity for a fixed generic Gröbner-elimination computation.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_G\) be the diagnostic polynomial obtained by clearing the denominators and retaining the leading coefficients of a Gröbner basis computed over \(k(p)\). The failure boundary of that computation is \(V(D_G)\). If \(D_G(a)\ne0\), specialization preserves the generic leading-term calculation. If \(D_G(a)=0\), at least one algebraic justification used by that calculation fails: a coefficient may be undefined, a leading term may disappear, or a reduction step may change. Consequently, conclusions about the elimination ideal, fiber dimension, or fiber degree must be recomputed for \(I_a\). Vanishing of \(D_G(a)\) is a failure of the generic certificate, not necessarily a failure of the desired conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the diagnostic zero set, generic elimination specializes correctly; on it, the generic certificate fails and the fiber must be recomputed.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed diagnostic polynomial is not shown to include every denominator and nonvanishing condition needed to specialize the Gröbner or elimination computation. The cited locator does not establish the claimed boundary, so the conclusions outside V(D_G) remain unreliable without a specialization theorem or comprehensive Gröbner-trace construction.

children.title: Real-Radical Computation
children.top_down_role: Symbolic and semidefinite interfaces for recovering real-radical closures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reconstruction from a certified exhaustive list of real algebraic roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subset\mathbb Q[x]\) be zero-dimensional. After computing exact algebraic representations of all complex roots and certifying the real roots, \[\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}=I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))=\bigcap_{a\in V_{\mathbb R}(I)}\mathfrak m_a.\] Exact minimal-polynomial and isolating data are required; floating-point approximations alone do not determine this intersection ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a zero-dimensional ideal, certify every real algebraic root and intersect its maximal ideal to reconstruct the real radical.
assumptions_latex: The real roots and completeness of the root list are certified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}=\bigcap_{a\in V_{\mathbb R}(I)}\mathfrak m_a.

notation.meaning: maximal ideal of polynomials vanishing at a

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Dimensional Real-Radical Reconstruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact SOS-identity semidecision for membership in a real radical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finitely generated ideal \(I\subset\mathbb R[x]\), \[f\in\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\iff\exists m\ge1,\ \exists\sigma\in\Sigma[x]:\ f^{2m}+\sigma\in I.\] Enumerating \(m\) and degree bounds for \(\sigma\), solving the corresponding SOS feasibility problems, and verifying any resulting polynomial identity exactly therefore semidecides membership. Failure at any finite search level is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerated SOS identities semidecide real-radical membership; a verified identity certifies membership, while finite failure proves nothing.
assumptions_latex: Candidate SOS and ideal identities are verified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\sqrt[\mathbb R]{I}\iff\exists m\ge1,\sigma\in\Sigma[x]:f^{2m}+\sigma\in I.

notation.meaning: cone of polynomial sums of squares

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Nullstellensatz Membership Semidecision

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reliability boundary for numerical real-radical reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite list of floating-point approximate roots and residuals does not certify \(I(V_{\mathbb R}(I))\): an omitted real root changes the intersection ideal, a nearly real conjugate pair can be misclassified, and approximate coefficient fitting need not yield an exact polynomial identity. Reconstruction is certified only after root existence, distinctness, reality, and completeness are validated and the reconstructed generators are verified exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate roots alone cannot certify a real radical; the roots and reconstructed identities require exact validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Uncertified approximate roots}\not\Rightarrow\text{a certified real-radical ideal}.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Root Reconstruction Boundary

assumptions_latex: SOS feasibility and exact ideal-membership tests are available at successively increasing degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(f\in\sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I}\), some finite search level finds \(m\) and \(\sigma\) satisfying \(f^{2m}+\sigma\in I\).

notation.meaning: Real radical of the equality ideal.
Cone of sums of squares in the polynomial ring.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidecision interface combining SOS searches with exact ideal membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x]\), enumerate integers \(m\ge1\) and degree bounds \(d\). At level \((m,d)\), solve the semidefinite feasibility problem of finding \(\sigma\in	ilde\Sigma[x]\) with \(\deg(\sigma)\le2d\) such that
\[
f^{2m}+\sigma\in I,
\]
where the displayed \(\tilde\Sigma[x]\) denotes the SOS cone \(\Sigma[x]\). Verify the resulting identity by exact polynomial reduction modulo generators or a Gröbner basis of \(I\). On verification, output that \(f\in\sqrt[\mathbb{R}]{I}\). The real Nullstellensatz makes this search complete for membership, while failure at any fixed \((m,d)\) is inconclusive. Applying the test to candidate generators yields certified portions of the real-radical closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate SOS identities and verify them exactly; a successful identity certifies real-radical membership, while finite-level failure is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.title: Real-Radical Computation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The real-Nullstellensatz semidecision principle is plausible, but no source supports either the membership equivalence or the algorithmic scope. The unexplained symbol \(\tilde\Sigma[x]\) also conflicts with the declared notation \(\Sigma[x]\).

children.title: Numerical Algebraic Geometry Interface
children.top_down_role: Numerical dimension, component, and singularity information used to assess equality assumptions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local certification of an approximate nonsingular zero, not completeness of a decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a square analytic system \(F\) and a point \(z\) with invertible Jacobian, define \(\beta(F,z)=\|J_F(z)^{-1}F(z)\|\), \(\gamma(F,z)=\sup_{m\ge2}\|J_F(z)^{-1}D^mF(z)/m!\|^{1/(m-1)}\), and \(\alpha(F,z)=\beta(F,z)\gamma(F,z)\). If a rigorously bounded \(\alpha(F,z)\) is below a valid universal threshold for the chosen norm and theorem version, Newton iteration converges quadratically to its associated nonsingular zero. This local certificate does not show that all zeros or components were found.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently small rigorously bounded alpha quantity certifies a nearby nonsingular root and quadratic Newton convergence, but not global completeness.
assumptions_latex: A rigorous gamma bound and a valid alpha threshold are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(F,z)<\alpha_0\Rightarrow z\text{ is an approximate zero associated with a locally certified nonsingular root}.
knowledge_statements.title: Alpha-Theoretic Local Root Certification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Witness Set for an Irreducible Component
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core numerical-algebraic representation of a positive-dimensional component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb C^n\) be an irreducible component of dimension \(d\) and degree \(\delta\). For a generic affine linear subspace \(L\) of codimension \(d\), \(W=X\cap L\) consists of \(\delta\) nonsingular transverse points. A numerical witness set is a triple \((F,L,W)\), where \(F\) vanishes on \(X\) and the points of \(W\) are represented numerically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A witness set represents a component by its degree-many intersections with a generic complementary linear space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |X\cap L|=\deg X\text{, with transverse intersection at nonsingular points}.
knowledge_statements.title: Witness Set for an Irreducible Component

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deflation Interface for Isolated Singular Roots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical regularization of an isolated singular solution without a global completeness claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an isolated singular zero \(x^*\) of a polynomial system \(F\), a deflation step augments the system with equations encoding a nonzero Jacobian-kernel vector and a normalization patch. Repeating valid deflation steps can produce an augmented system having a nonsingular lifted zero above \(x^*\), after which nonsingular-root certification may be applied to the lifted system. Deflation does not by itself certify that the original solution list is complete, and an invalid normalization patch or unverified numerical rank can invalidate the lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deflation can turn an isolated singular root into a nonsingular lifted root for local certification, but it does not certify global completeness.
assumptions_latex: Each numerical rank decision and normalization patch used by deflation is valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A successfully deflated lift may be certified as a nonsingular zero projecting to }x^*.

notation.meaning: isolated singular zero of the original system

knowledge_statements.title: Deflation Interface for Isolated Singular Roots

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Numerical Irreducible Decomposition by Witness Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard component-decomposition interface with explicit numerical completeness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each dimension \(d\), intersect \(V(F)\subset\mathbb C^n\) with generic affine subspaces of codimension \(d\), track the isolated slice solutions through generic homotopies, and partition the endpoints using monodromy and trace tests. Under complete start data, generic slices, successful tracking of every required path, and validated trace tests, the resulting witness-set blocks represent the numerical irreducible components. Certified path tracking validates the paths it follows but does not by itself prove that the initial witness superset or component list was complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generic slicing, continuation, monodromy, and trace tests yield a numerical irreducible decomposition only under explicit start-data and path-completeness conditions.
assumptions_latex: The slices and homotopies are generic.
All required start solutions are supplied.
Every required path is successfully tracked.
The trace tests are validated at adequate precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting witness-set partition represents the numerically irreducible components under the stated completeness conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Irreducible Decomposition by Witness Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete conditioning boundary for numerical singularity diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_\varepsilon(x)=x(x-\varepsilon)\) with \(\varepsilon\ne0\), the roots \(0\) and \(\varepsilon\) are distinct and nonsingular because \(F_\varepsilon'(0)=-\varepsilon\) and \(F_\varepsilon'(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\). A numerical rule declaring derivatives of magnitude at most \(\tau\) to be zero misclassifies both roots as singular whenever \(0<|\varepsilon|\le\tau\); insufficient spatial resolution may also merge them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two arbitrarily close simple roots can be labeled singular or merged by a fixed numerical threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A threshold-based Jacobian test may report singularity although both roots are algebraically simple.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Rank Misclassification

assumptions_latex: Numerical continuation, rank estimation, and residual tolerances are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The numerical output supplies diagnostics for equality assumptions, but it is not an exact algebraic certificate without certified error bounds or symbolic reconstruction.

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of the defining system.
Numerically represented witness sets for components of dimension d.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic, rather than automatically certifying, use of numerical algebraic geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical algebraic geometry interface computes witness sets \(W_d\) for numerically irreducible components of \(V(F)\), estimates their dimensions and degrees, and evaluates ranks of \(J_F(x)\) at sampled points. A rank drop relative to the expected codimension flags possible singularity or nonreduced structure; positive-dimensional witness sets refute a zero-dimensional equality assumption. These conclusions are conditional on continuation accuracy, rank thresholds, and component completeness. They become exact certificates only after certified path tracking, interval or alpha-theoretic validation, or symbolic reconstruction verifies the asserted solutions, dimensions, and rank conditions. Uncertified numerical absence of a component or singularity does not establish algebraic absence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Witness sets and Jacobian ranks diagnose dimension, components, and singularities, but exact equality assumptions require certified or symbolic validation.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Algebraic Geometry Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagnostic-versus-certified distinction fits the container, but witness-set completeness, numerical irreducible decomposition, rank interpretation, and the listed certification mechanisms require an inspectable numerical algebraic geometry source.

children.title: Equality-Aware Reduction Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Equality-aware reductions affecting certificate size and moment representation.

children.title: Normal-Form Reduction
children.top_down_role: Polynomial reduction modulo equality relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical polynomial representative for a fixed Gröbner basis and monomial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Multivariate division of \(f\) by \(G\) gives
\[
f=\sum_{g\in G}q_g g+r,
\]
where no monomial of \(r\) is divisible by a leading monomial of an element of \(G\). Because \(G\) is a Gröbner basis, this normal form is unique for the fixed monomial order; define \(\operatorname{NF}_G(f):=r\). Thus \(f+I=r+I\) in \(k[x]/I\), and \(f\in I\) if and only if \(r=0\). Replacing a polynomial expression by its normal form performs equality-aware reduction without changing its residue class modulo \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Division by a Gröbner basis gives the unique normal-form representative of a polynomial modulo the equality ideal.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subset k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is an ideal, and \(G\) is a Gröbner basis of \(I\) for a fixed monomial order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\equiv\operatorname{NF}_G(f)\pmod I\), and \(f\in I\) if and only if \(\operatorname{NF}_G(f)=0\).

notation.meaning: Unique Gröbner normal form of a polynomial.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noncanonical Remainders without a Gröbner Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why an arbitrary ideal generating set does not define canonical reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(k[x,y]\), fix a monomial order with \(\operatorname{LM}(xy-1)=xy\) and \(\operatorname{LM}(y^2-y)=y^2\). For \[G=\{xy-1,\ y^2-y\},\qquad f=xy^2,\] valid reduction choices produce the distinct terminal remainders \(y\) and \(1\). These remainders represent the same residue class modulo \(\langle G\rangle\), but they are unequal. Thus this non-Gröbner generating set does not define a unique normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Division by a non-Gröbner generating set can return different irreducible remainders and therefore is not canonical.
assumptions_latex: The displayed leading monomials are taken under one fixed monomial order.
Reduction may choose any currently applicable divisor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(G\) yields distinct terminal remainders \(y\) and \(1\) for \(f\).

notation.meaning: Leading monomial under the fixed monomial order.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncanonical Remainders without a Gröbner Basis

children.title: Quotient-Basis Selection
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-basis choices for finite-dimensional quotient algebras.

assumptions_latex: A monomial order and a Gröbner basis \(G\) of \(I\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residue classes of \(B\) form a basis of \(k[x]/I\), with \(|B|=\dim_k(k[x]/I)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-monomial basis for a zero-dimensional polynomial quotient.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the standard-monomial set
\[
B:=\{x^\alpha:x^\alpha\notin\operatorname{LT}(I)\}.
\]
Because \(I\) is zero-dimensional, \(B\) is finite. The residue classes \(\{b+I:b\in B\}\) form a \(k\)-basis of \(A=k[x]/I\). Every \(f+I\in A\) therefore has the unique coordinate representation
\[
f+I=\sum_{b\in B}c_b(b+I),
\]
obtained from \(\operatorname{NF}_G(f)\). Hence quotient-basis selection converts multiplication modulo the equality ideal into finite multiplication matrices; changing the monomial order may change \(B\) and conditioning, but not \(\dim_k A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard monomials outside the leading-term ideal form a finite coordinate basis for a zero-dimensional quotient algebra.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Basis Selection

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplication Matrices in a Quotient Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the finite linear-algebra representation induced by a chosen basis of a zero-dimensional quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\) be finite-dimensional with ordered basis \(B\). Define \(X_i\) by \[X_i[f+I]_B=[x_i f+I]_B.\] The matrices \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) commute, and multiplication by \(p+I\) is represented by \(p(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\). If \([a]_C=S^{-1}[a]_B\) for another basis \(C\), then \[X_i^{(C)}=S^{-1}X_i^{(B)}S.\] Thus quotient dimension and multiplication are basis invariant, while sparsity and numerical conditioning may depend on the selected coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient basis turns coordinate multiplication into commuting matrices, and basis changes simultaneously conjugate those matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate multiplication matrices commute and transform by simultaneous similarity under quotient-basis changes.

notation.meaning: Matrix of multiplication by the residue class of coordinate x_i.
Coordinate vector of a quotient class in basis B.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplication Matrices in a Quotient Basis

children.title: Equality-Reduced Moment Models
children.top_down_role: Moment representations compressed by polynomial equality relations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends equality-reduced moment matrices to inequalities without restoring redundant equality coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\mathbb R[x]/I\) be finite-dimensional with basis \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)\), and let \(L:A\to\mathbb R\) be linear. For \(g\in\mathbb R[x]\), define \[M_B(gL)_{ij}=L(gb_i b_j+I).\] For \(q=\sum_i c_i b_i\), \(c^{\mathsf T}M_B(gL)c=L(gq^2+I)\). Hence \(M_B(gL)\succeq0\) is equivalent to nonnegativity of \(L\) on every class \(gq^2+I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality is localized in the equality quotient by reducing products g b_i b_j modulo the ideal and imposing positive semidefiniteness.
assumptions_latex: \(A=\mathbb R[x]/I\) is finite-dimensional and \(B\) is a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_B(gL)\succeq0\iff L(gq^2+I)\ge0\) for every \(q+I\in A\).

notation.meaning: Inequality-localizing matrix in the quotient basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Localizing Matrices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Atomic Representation on a Finite Real Variety
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes positive quotient functionals for the vanishing ideal of finitely many real points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{u_1,\ldots,u_s\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(I=I(V)\). Every linear functional \(L:\mathbb R[x]/I\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(L(q^2+I)\ge0\) for all \(q\) has a unique representation \[L(f+I)=\sum_{k=1}^s w_k f(u_k),\qquad w_k\ge0.\] If \(L(1)=1\), then \(\sum_k w_k=1\). If quotient-localizing positivity is also imposed for inequalities \(g_i\ge0\), every weight at a point violating some inequality is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive functional on the coordinate algebra of a finite real variety is a unique nonnegative weighted sum of point evaluations, with localizing positivity excluding infeasible atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is nonnegative on squares in \(\mathbb R[x]/I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\sum_{k=1}^s w_k\operatorname{ev}_{u_k}\) with unique weights \(w_k\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Ideal of all polynomials vanishing on V.

knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Representation on a Finite Real Variety
Equality-Reduced Moment Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite quotient-algebra moment representation for zero-dimensional equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)\) and define the equality-reduced moment matrix by
\[
M_B(L)_{ij}:=L\bigl((b_i+I)(b_j+I)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, when a Gröbner basis \(G\) of \(I\) is fixed, the entry is \(L(\operatorname{NF}_G(b_i b_j)+I)\). For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^N\), let \(q:=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i b_i\). Then
\[
c^{\mathsf T}M_B(L)c=L(q^2+I)\ge 0,
\]
so \(M_B(L)\succeq0\). Because \(h+I=0\) for every \(h\in I\), equality relations are absorbed by the quotient rather than imposed as separate moment equations. Polynomial inequalities, when present, require additional localizing conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Products reduced in a quotient basis define a positive semidefinite moment matrix and enforce every polynomial equality in the ideal identically.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subset\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is zero-dimensional, and \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)\) has residue classes forming a basis of \(A=\mathbb{R}[x]/I\).
\(L:A\to\mathbb{R}\) is linear and satisfies \(L(q^2+I)\ge0\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}[x]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_B(L)\succeq0\), and every relation in \(I\) is enforced identically through computation in \(A\).

notation.meaning: Moment matrix indexed by the quotient basis.

children.title: Certificate Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural sources of certificate-size growth and limits on effective assumption verification.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications

children.title: Quadratic-Module–Preordering Size Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Certificate strength versus generator-product growth across the principal inequality containers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A univariate instance shows that same-order module inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1=x\), \(g_2=1-x\), and truncate both containers at degree two. Then \[x(1-x)\in T_1(g)\setminus M_1(g).\] The preordering membership uses the square-free product \(g_1g_2\); no degree-two quadratic-module representation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the interval generators x and 1−x, their product has a degree-two preordering certificate but no degree-two quadratic-module certificate.
assumptions_latex: Both containers use the total-degree-two truncation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(1-x)\in T_1(g)\setminus M_1(g)\).

notation.meaning: Quadratic module truncated at degree two.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Fixed-Order Preordering Advantage

assumptions_latex: All SOS multipliers are truncated so that every displayed term has degree at most \(2d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_d(g)\subseteq T_d(g)\); the preordering may be stronger but introduces up to \(2^m\) generator-product families instead of \(m+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-degree comparison of SOS certificate strength and generator-product growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The truncated quadratic module and preordering are
\[
M_d(g):=\left\{\sigma_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g_i:\sigma_i\in\Sigma[x],\ \deg(\sigma_i g_i)\le2d\right\},
\]
\[
T_d(g):=\left\{\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^m}\sigma_\alpha g^\alpha:\sigma_\alpha\in\Sigma[x],\ \deg(\sigma_\alpha g^\alpha)\le2d\right\}.
\]
Choosing only \(\alpha=0\) and unit vectors shows \(M_d(g)\subseteq T_d(g)\). Thus a preordering can supply certificates unavailable to the same-order quadratic module, but it can require SOS or localizing blocks for as many as \(2^m\) square-free generator products, versus \(m+1\) multiplier families for the quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preorderings contain quadratic modules at the same degree but may require exponentially many square-free generator-product blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Module–Preordering Size Tradeoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The same-degree inclusion and square-free-product count are standard and fit the size-tradeoff container, but no source is supplied for the truncated definitions or comparison.

children.title: Description-Sensitive Relaxation Size
children.top_down_role: Dependence of finite certificate models on generator count, degree, and equality representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Size of a Dense SOS Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts dense PSD variables and coefficient equations induced by a fixed generator description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At relaxation order \(d\), set \(g_0=1\), \(e_i=\deg g_i\), \(d_i=d-\lceil e_i/2\rceil\), and \(s_i=\binom{n+d_i}{d_i}\) for each \(d_i\ge0\). A dense Gram realization of \(\sigma_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g_i\), with \(\deg(\sigma_i g_i)\le2d\), has PSD blocks of orders \(s_i\), containing \(\sum_{i:d_i\ge0}s_i(s_i+1)/2\) scalar symmetric-matrix entries before linear dependencies or sparsity reductions. Matching an identity of degree at most \(2d\) introduces at most \(\binom{n+2d}{2d}\) scalar coefficient equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense SOS model size is the sum of the triangular Gram-block sizes, with at most one coefficient equation per monomial through degree 2d.
assumptions_latex: A dense total-degree monomial basis and the truncation \(\deg(\sigma_i g_i)\le2d\) are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unreduced PSD-entry count is \(\sum_{i:d_i\ge0}s_i(s_i+1)/2\), and the coefficient-equation count is at most \(\binom{n+2d}{2d}\).

notation.meaning: Maximum monomial degree in the SOS Gram basis for multiplier i.
Order of the corresponding dense Gram block.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Size of a Dense SOS Relaxation

assumptions_latex: Polynomials in \(n\) variables are represented in the monomial basis.
An SOS relaxation uses polynomials of degree at most \(2d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unreduced SOS Gram block has order \(\binom{n+d}{d}\); generator degrees and quotient relations change the number and orders of all blocks.

notation.meaning: Vector of monomials of degree at most d.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial SDP size induced by degree, generators, and equality reduction.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A polynomial SOS of degree at most \(2d\) has a Gram representation \(v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x)\) with \(Q\succeq0\) of order
\[
s(n,d)=\binom{n+d}{d}.
\]
For a multiplier of a generator \(g_i\) having degree \(e_i\), the corresponding block uses monomials through degree \(d-\lceil e_i/2\rceil\), when this number is nonnegative. Thus both block count and block orders depend on the chosen generator list and its degrees. If equalities define a quotient and reduction is valid, replacing monomials by an independent truncated quotient basis reduces each order to the dimension of the relevant quotient subspace; redundant or high-degree descriptions can enlarge the unreduced model without changing the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation size depends combinatorially on degree and variables, while generator degrees and quotient relations determine block count and reduced dimensions.
knowledge_statements.title: Description-Sensitive Relaxation Size

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gram-block count is standard, but the cited elementary-algebraic-geometry locator does not support SOS Gram sizing, multiplier block orders, or quotient-reduced SDP dimensions. A specific SOS or moment-relaxation source is required.

children.title: Hardness of Assumption Recognition
children.top_down_role: Computational boundaries for detecting boundedness, exactness, and related certificate properties.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact decidability of geometric recognition from its worst-case hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_j(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\ge0\}\), nonemptiness is the first-order sentence \(\exists x\,(x\in K)\), while boundedness is expressed by \[\exists R\ge0\;\forall x\;\left(x\in K\Rightarrow\sum_{k=1}^n x_k^2\le R^2\right).\] For exact rational input, quantifier elimination over real closed fields decides both sentences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Real quantifier elimination exactly decides nonemptiness and boundedness of rational semialgebraic descriptions, although it need not be efficient.
assumptions_latex: All input coefficients are rational and represented exactly.
The boundedness question concerns the described real set, not Archimedeanity of a selected quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonemptiness and boundedness of \(K\) are decidable by real quantifier elimination.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Decidability of Semialgebraic Boundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective enumeration of finite ball certificates over exact rational polynomial data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(g)\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\) be generated by rational polynomials \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\). Enumerate integers \(N\ge1\) and degree bounds \(2d\). For each pair, decide feasibility of \[N-\|x\|_2^2=\sigma_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g_i,\qquad \sigma_i\in\Sigma[x],\qquad \deg(\sigma_i g_i)\le2d,\] using an exact first-order real decision procedure on Gram-matrix variables. If \(M(g)\) is Archimedean, some enumerated pair is feasible and the procedure halts with a ball certificate. No termination is guaranteed for non-Archimedean input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Archimedeanity is positively semidecidable by enumerating ball radii and certificate degrees and exactly testing the resulting finite SOS systems.
assumptions_latex: The generators have exact rational coefficients.
SOS feasibility is decided over real Gram matrices by an exact real-algebraic procedure.
Archimedeanity is interpreted through containment of a polynomial ball bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The enumeration halts with a valid certificate for every Archimedean input but may run forever otherwise.

notation.meaning: Quadratic module generated by the input polynomials

knowledge_statements.title: Semidecision Procedure for Archimedeanity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Decidability of Fixed-Order SOS Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition boundary when the certificate degree is fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given rational polynomials \(p,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) and a fixed degree bound \(2d\), membership \[p\in M_d(g):=\left\{\sigma_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g_i:\sigma_i\in\Sigma[x],\ \deg(\sigma_i g_i)\le2d\right\}\] is expressible as existence of finitely many positive-semidefinite Gram matrices satisfying rational linear coefficient-matching equations. Positive semidefiniteness is semialgebraic, so exact quantifier elimination over real closed fields decides membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a specified relaxation order, exact quadratic-module membership is decidable through finite Gram-matrix feasibility over the reals.
assumptions_latex: All polynomial coefficients are rational and exact.
The truncation degree \(2d\) and finite monomial bases are part of the input instance.
The question is exact certificate membership, not approximate numerical SDP feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision problem \(p\in M_d(g)\) is decidable by real quantifier elimination.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Decidability of Fixed-Order SOS Membership

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case recognition boundary for arbitrary exactly encoded polynomial systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given integer polynomials \(h_j,g_i\) encoded in binary, deciding whether \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_j(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\ge0\}\] is nonempty is complete for \(\exists\mathbb R\) under polynomial-time many-one reductions. Consequently, any general assumption-recognition problem whose required output includes deciding nonemptiness of arbitrary such descriptions is \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hard. This transfer does not by itself classify compactness, Archimedeanity, radicality, or finite convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General certificate-assumption analysis inherits existential-theory-of-the-reals hardness whenever it must decide feasibility of arbitrary polynomial descriptions.
assumptions_latex: Input polynomial coefficients are integers encoded in binary.
The number of variables, constraints, and polynomial degrees are unrestricted input parameters.
Hardness is under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semialgebraic nonemptiness is \(\exists\mathbb R\)-complete, and any recognition task containing it is \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hard.

notation.meaning: Complexity class of problems polynomial-time reducible to existential real feasibility

knowledge_statements.title: Existential-Theory-of-the-Reals Feasibility Boundary

assumptions_latex: Input polynomials have integer or rational coefficients encoded in binary.
Recognition is required for arbitrary finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General recognition tasks that include deciding whether \(K\ne\varnothing\) are \(\exists\mathbb{R}\)-hard under polynomial-time reductions.

notation.meaning: Existential theory of the reals complexity class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case bit-complexity boundary for general semialgebraic assumption recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_j(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\ge0\}.
\]
Deciding whether \(K\ne\varnothing\) is the canonical existential theory of the reals problem and is \(\exists\mathbb{R}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. Therefore any general recognition problem whose required output includes correct detection of nonemptiness for arbitrary polynomial descriptions is \(\exists\mathbb{R}\)-hard. Certificate-assumption analyzers that first require feasibility cannot have a uniformly easier worst-case decision procedure unless additional structure is imposed. This statement does not by itself classify recognition of compactness, Archimedeanness, radicality, or finite convergence; each is a distinct decision problem and requires its own reduction and encoding conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General assumption recognition already inherits existential-theory-of-reals hardness when it must decide feasibility of arbitrary polynomial systems.
knowledge_statements.title: Hardness of Assumption Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scoped hardness statement is plausible and appropriately avoids classifying the other recognition problems, but the \(\exists\mathbb{R}\)-completeness claim and encoding/reduction model require an authoritative complexity source.

children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of radicality, rank, singularity, and strict-feasibility diagnostics to finite precision.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Separation Certificate for Stable Numerical Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the margin required for a perturbation-stable numerical-rank conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) have singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p(A)\). Suppose \(\sigma_r(A)>2\delta\), \(\sigma_{r+1}(A)=0\), and \(\|E\|_2<\delta\). Then \(\sigma_r(A+E)>\delta\) and \(\sigma_{r+1}(A+E)<\delta\). Hence thresholding the singular values of \(A+E\) at \(\delta\) returns numerical rank \(r\). This conclusion concerns thresholded numerical rank, not exact rank of the perturbed matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified error bound and singular-value gap certify stable numerical rank; thresholding alone does not certify exact rank.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(E\) are real matrices of the same size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly \(r\) singular values of \(A+E\) exceed \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: The ith largest singular value of A.
Certified perturbation bound and numerical-rank threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Separation Certificate for Stable Numerical Rank

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-parameter semidefinite family separates strict feasibility, boundary feasibility, and infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A_\varepsilon(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,\varepsilon-t)\), the system \(A_\varepsilon(t)\succeq0\) is strictly feasible when \(\varepsilon>0\), has only the singular feasible matrix \(A_0(0)=0\) when \(\varepsilon=0\), and is infeasible when \(\varepsilon<0\). Thus arbitrarily small changes in \(\varepsilon\) can switch among strict feasibility, boundary-only feasibility, and infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrarily small scalar perturbation can switch an SDP among strict feasibility, singular feasibility, and infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility means that some \(t\in\mathbb R\) satisfies \(A_\varepsilon(t)\succeq0\).
Strict feasibility means that some \(t\) satisfies \(A_\varepsilon(t)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility has no uniform perturbation margin at \(\varepsilon=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuous Strict-Feasibility Diagnostic
Numerical Fragility of Algebraic Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete discontinuity of algebraic and rank predicates at degenerate data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(I_\varepsilon=\langle x^2-\varepsilon\rangle\subset\mathbb{R}[x]\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), the ideal is nonradical and its real variety is the singular point \(\{0\}\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the ideal is radical and has two nonsingular real roots; for every \(\varepsilon<0\), its real variety is empty and its real radical is the unit ideal. Thus arbitrarily small coefficient perturbations can change radicality, real-root count, singularity, and real-radical closure. Likewise, \(A_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\) has rank one at \(\varepsilon=0\) and rank two when \(\varepsilon\ne0\), while its smallest singular value is \(|\varepsilon|\). Finite-precision thresholds therefore cannot uniformly certify these exact predicates near the degenerate instances without separation bounds or validated error estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degenerate polynomial and matrix families show that arbitrarily small perturbations can change radicality, real roots, singularity, real-radical closure, and exact rank.
assumptions_latex: Polynomial coefficients and matrix entries may be perturbed by arbitrarily small real amounts.
Diagnostics use exact radicality, real-root, singularity, real-radical, or rank predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No uniform positive perturbation radius preserves all the displayed predicates near \(I_0\) and \(A_0\).
